evidence.description: addGroupMembers throws 'Membership ... is maintained automatically' for group.system - updateGroup rewrites the same table rows unguarded.
bulkSetRequestable's editable set filters g.system - the invariant is applied everywhere except updateGroup.
reconcileWatchlist restores group_members from user_watch on sweep/flag events - divergence self-heals, bounding the effect.
Console members array unions existing members with form additions - injection is possible, removal is not, on this path.

conditions.description: Caller holds groups:write (console role or API key) below super-admin - the delegated directory tier.
Injected membership lasts until the next reconcile (hourly sweep or next flag operation); the SCIM push of the forged state is immediate.

execution.attacker_perspective: A delegated directory administrator (groups:write) who should not control the code-maintained risk watchlist.
payloads: POST /admin/groups/{watchlistId} with an added user in the members field (console)
PATCH /api/v1/groups/{watchlistId} { requestable: true }
instructions: Find the watchlist group's id via the groups list (groups:read).
Submit a group update adding a chosen user: group_members gains them and the post-write sync pushes the forged membership to SCIM targets.
Observe reconcileWatchlist (hourly or on next flag change) removes them again - meanwhile downstream consumers saw them as risk-flagged.
execution.observed_result: group_members of the system group reflects caller input rather than live user_watch rows until reconcile; SCIM targets already received the forged membership.

remediation.strategy: In updateGroup, when current.system is set refuse the update (mirroring deleteGroup) or at least refuse changes that touch members/requestable, so the 'maintained by code' invariant holds on every mutation path.

code_changes.fixed_code: if (current.system) throw new ServiceError(400, `"${current.name}" is a system group and cannot be edited.`);

likelihood.reason: groups:write is a normal delegated tier and the write is one call.

impact.reason: Windowed divergence that self-heals on reconcile; the immediate SCIM push is the residual effect - a detection-integrity weakening, not access grant.

confidence.reason: Missing guard plus five sibling guards enforcing the same invariant read directly; both caller paths traced.

title: IdP signs `email_verified:true` unconditionally and `phone_number_verified`/`address` claims from self-service-writable schema attributes
description: buildClaims (src/lib/jwt.ts) emits verification assertions FlareID never performs. (1) Line 71: whenever the `email` claim group is released, `email_verified: true` is hardcoded - the product has no email-verification state or flow at all, and the value asserted is user.upn verbatim (token.ts:327), which prior confirmed record services.users.identity-field-admission established can be an arbitrary non-address string, so RPs can receive email_verified:true next to a value that is not even an email address. (2) Lines 76-80: `phone_number` and `phone_number_verified` are assembled from custom_attributes - schema attributes that an administrator can flag user_editable, in which case the end user writes them via POST /account/profile (account.ts:787-807); a user setting phone_number_verified="true" gets an IdP-signed claim asserting the phone was verified. (3) Lines 46-55: the `address` claim emits parsed JSON from the user-writable `address` attribute verbatim, so its member set is entirely user-controlled (and a JSON array value passes the typeof==='object' check and is emitted as a malformed array claim). The trust boundary crossed is OP-to-RP attestation accuracy: OIDC Core 5.1.2 defines *_verified claims as the OP's statement that it verified the value, and RPs (notably ones doing email_verified-based account linking) rely on it.
root_cause: src/lib/jwt.ts:71 hardcodes email_verified:true with no verification state in the data model, and lines 46-80 source the phone_number_verified flag and the whole address object from custom_attributes that the self-service profile editor (account.ts:793-806) writes whenever the schema administrator marked the attribute user_editable - there is no distinction between provisioner-attested and user-asserted values when claims are assembled.
intended_behavior: Verification claims should reflect an actual verification decision: emit email_verified only when the address was verified (or omit/false otherwise), never source a *_verified flag from a self-service-writable attribute, and constrain the address claim to the Core 5.1.1 member set regardless of what JSON a user supplies.

trace.description: User writes every schema attribute the admin flagged user_editable into users.custom_attributes, including names like phone_number_verified and address.
phone_number_verified is emitted as customAttributes.phone_number_verified === 'true'; the address claim is JSON.parse(attrs.address) emitted verbatim as a claim object.
email_verified:true is emitted unconditionally beside email=user.upn (token.ts:327) for every token and /userinfo response releasing the email group.

evidence.description: Object.assign(attributes, { email: claims.email, email_verified: true }) - the literal true; no verification field exists on users or elsewhere to source it from.
attributes.phone_number_verified = claims.customAttributes.phone_number_verified === 'true' - a self-service-writable string becomes an IdP verification assertion.
JSON.parse(attrs.address) returned verbatim as the address claim when it parses to any object (including arrays); user-supplied JSON controls the claim's members.

conditions.description: The phone/address vector requires the schema administrator to have declared a user_editable attribute named phone_number_verified/address (plausible standard naming); email_verified is unconditional.
Concrete harm requires a relying party that trusts *_verified claims for a security decision such as automatic account linking on verified email/phone.

execution.attacker_perspective: A low-privilege FlareID user at a deployment whose schema marks phone_number_verified user-editable, targeting an RP that skips its own verification when the OP asserts it.
payloads: POST /account/profile attr_phone_number_verified=true&attr_phone_number=%2B15555550100
POST /account/profile attr_address=%7B%22street_address%22%3A%22x%22%2C%22anything%22%3A%22y%22%7D
instructions: Set a user_editable phone_number_verified attribute to the string 'true' via POST /account/profile.
Complete an authorization for a client allowed the phone group (claims or scope=phone) and inspect the issued id_token/userinfo: phone_number_verified:true is signed by the OP.
Independently, any client receiving email scope always sees email_verified:true regardless of whether any verification occurred.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified: email_verified is a literal true (jwt.ts:71); phone_number_verified and the address claim are direct projections of self-service-writable custom attributes (jwt.ts:46-80 fed by account.ts:793-806).

remediation.strategy: Stop asserting unverified states: emit email_verified only from a real verification flag (or omit it), exclude *_verified-suffixed and claim-assembly attribute names from user_editable schema attributes (or strip them at buildClaims), and whitelist address claim members to the Core 5.1.1 set after parsing.

likelihood.reason: The self-service vector needs an editable *_verified/address attribute; the email_verified misattestation is unconditional but needs an RP that acts on it, and user UPNs are provisioner-controlled so the email value itself is not user-chosen.

impact.reason: A signed false attestation can steer an RP's verification or linking decision; bounded to claim-integrity, no direct account access demonstrated from FlareID's side.

confidence.reason: The code paths are direct: literal-true email_verified, and verbatim projections of self-service-writable attributes into verification claims; only the deployment schema and RP reliance are conditional.

title: 'One-shot' credentials are claimed by KV get-then-delete - deletes propagate for up to ~60s, so SAML assertions, OIDC states and passkey challenges replay
description: Several security-critical single-use checks are implemented as `KV.get` followed by `KV.delete`. Cloudflare KV is eventually consistent (deletes and edge-cached reads propagate for up to ~60 seconds) and get->delete is non-atomic anyway, so the same one-shot value is returned to additional callers both concurrently AND sequentially inside the propagation window. Sites: (a) takeFedState (src/lib/federation.ts:174-179) - consumed by the SAML ACS (src/routes/federation.ts:141) and the OIDC callback (:109); replaying a captured SAMLResponse+RelayState within the window passes the state check again and verifySamlResponse still succeeds (same signed response, valid InResponseTo, fresh time bounds), minting another session as the victim at :156; the OIDC callback replay is backstopped only by the upstream's one-use code. (b) WebAuthn challenge takes (src/lib/passkeys.ts:79-81,113-115) - a captured assertion replays while the challenge remains readable; the cloned-authenticator check at :130 is skipped entirely for authenticators that always report sign_count 0 (platform passkeys), so there is no second gate. (c) SAML inbound AuthnRequest-ID single-use (src/routes/saml.ts:55,141) and SLO markers (src/routes/saml-slo.ts:89) are check-then-put on the same KV - replays inside the window mint a second signed response (login-CSRF-grade). (d) takePendingAction (src/lib/step-up.ts:98-107) - the stashed sensitive admin POST can double-execute for the same session. (e) pending-MFA and email-OTP takes (authorize-state.ts:189-213, email-otp.ts:107-129) share the pattern. The codebase already learned this lesson for rate limits: migrations/0007_security_audit.sql:1-5 replaced KV get/increment/put with an atomic INSERT .. ON CONFLICT .. DO UPDATE .. RETURNING 'because a get/increment/put pair could lose increments'.
root_cause: src/lib/federation.ts:174-179 (and the sibling take/check-then-set sites) treat KV as strongly consistent and atomic; KV guarantees neither, so 'consumed on read' is best-effort for ~60s.
intended_behavior: One-shot credentials must be claimed atomically in D1 (INSERT .. ON CONFLICT .. DO UPDATE .. RETURNING, the pattern already used for rate_limits and claimTotpCounter), not via KV get->delete.

trace.description: Attacker replays a captured SAMLResponse + RelayState POST body within the KV propagation window.
SESSIONS_KV.get returns the state again: the earlier delete has not propagated (or races it).
The replayed response still verifies - signature, InResponseTo and time bounds are unchanged.
finishFederatedLogin issues a second session for the victim's resolved account.

evidence.description: get-then-delete 'one-shot' comment - KV provides neither atomicity nor read-your-delete within ~60s.
Same take pattern for WebAuthn challenges; sign_count check at :130 does not fire for zero-counter authenticators.
AuthnRequest-ID replay check is a KV get whose put lands at :56 - check-then-set across the propagation window.
Migration comment documents the same non-atomicity lesson for rate_limits - KV get/put lost increments.
takePendingAction shares the pattern; impact bounded to the owning session.

conditions.description: SAML path requires a copy of the victim's ACS POST body (TLS-terminating proxy logs, browser extension, shared-device artifact); the window is ~60s after first use.
All paths depend on KV edge-cache/propagation delay; exploitability is highest across regions and concurrent requests, possible sequentially within the window.

execution.attacker_perspective: An attacker who can observe or harvest the victim's federation callback (SAML POST body or OIDC callback URL) or a WebAuthn assertion.
payloads: Re-POST the captured RelayState + SAMLResponse to /federation/saml/acs/{id}
Re-GET the captured /federation/oidc/callback?state=..&code=.. (works only if the upstream tolerates code reuse)
instructions: Capture the victim's ACS POST (or induce a second POST inside the window).
Replay it to /federation/saml/acs/:id: takeFedState returns the state again because the delete has not propagated.
The response verifies and finishFederatedLogin mints a session for the victim's account in the attacker's browser.
execution.observed_result: Second session issued for the same identity; audit shows two login.success rows for one upstream authentication.

remediation.strategy: Move one-shot claims to D1 with an atomic claim statement (INSERT .. ON CONFLICT .. DO NOTHING then check meta.changes, as rate_limits does), and keep KV only as a hint. Alternatively re-verify a server-side consumed flag in D1 before issuing sessions. Sibling sites (pending-action same-session double-execute, email OTP, pending-MFA, saml:req/slo markers) share the root and fix; the SAML ACS path is the demonstrable exploit.

code_changes.fixed_code: Replace KV get->delete with `INSERT INTO fed_state_claims(key, expires_at) VALUES (?, ?) ON CONFLICT(key) DO NOTHING` and proceed only when meta.changes === 1, storing the state payload in D1 (or KV as a cache).

likelihood.reason: Needs a captured federation POST/assertion plus replay inside the propagation window; capture paths exist (endpoint proxies, extensions) but are not free.

impact.reason: Successful replay mints an IdP session as the victim - full impersonation at FlareID and downstream RPs for that session.

confidence.reason: The get->delete pattern and the ACS/session-minting path are directly readable; KV's eventual consistency is documented Cloudflare behaviour. Exploit reachability hinges on capture, which lowers likelihood not the defect's reality.

title: LDAP compare builds every entry in the app view per operation (and viewForApp is O(users x app-groups x members)) - a bound credential turns one op into full-directory work with no time bound
description: Two compounding per-op costs on the LDAP plane: (1) executeCompare calls candidateEntries (src/ldap/search.ts:295-301), which eagerly builds userEntry for every user and groupEntry for every group in the app view - groupEntry awaits uuidV5 (SHA-1 digest, entries.ts:134) per group - then discards all but the one matching DN. Unlike executeSearch, which checks a deadline per candidate (search.ts:136-143, capped at 30s), the compare path has no deadline check: a single compare op costs O(|view|) entry materialisation plus one SHA-1 per group. (2) viewForApp (src/ldap/directory.ts:60-68) computes visibleUserIds by scanning snapshot.groups.some(g => userGroups.includes(g.id) && members.get(g.id).includes(u.id)) for every user - O(users x bind-groups x group-members) with linear Array.includes scans - and runs inside searchCtx (connection.ts:377-381) on every search AND every compare, because only the raw snapshot is cached (30s TTL, connection.ts:63-68), not the derived view. On a directory with app bind-groups configured, 10k users x 5 groups x 10k members is ~5e8 comparisons per op. A credential that can bind (LDAP app secret, or a user in the app's bind groups) can issue pipelined ops (MAX_OPS 10,000 per connection, connection.ts:55) to keep the isolate burning CPU.
root_cause: src/ldap/search.ts:295-301 materialises the whole view for a single-DN compare instead of resolving the one entry, and src/ldap/directory.ts:60-68 evaluates membership with nested linear scans per op instead of set-based lookups or a cached derived view.
intended_behavior: Compare should resolve just the named entry (or at minimum share executeSearch's per-candidate deadline), and the app view should be derived once per snapshot, not per operation.

trace.scope: compare op on a bound LDAP connection
trace.description: Any bound principal (service secret or app-group user) can send compare ops.
viewForApp runs per op over the full cached snapshot - quadratic visible-user filter.
Per-user scan of every app bind group's member list via Array.includes.
Full userEntry/groupEntry materialisation incl. uuidV5 SHA-1 per group - for a compare that uses at most one entry, with no deadline.

evidence.description: executeSearch caps work at 30s via a per-candidate deadline; executeCompare's loop has no equivalent.
Dynamic-group members resolved by filtering all users per rule - already O(users x dynamic-groups) inside the snapshot.
MAX_OPS 10_000 - a single connection can repeat the expensive op ten thousand times.

conditions.description: Requires a usable LDAP credential (app secret or in-scope user password); LDAP is opt-in per deployment and typically provisioner-network-facing.
Cost is proportional to directory size and bind-group membership; trivial on small directories, severe on large ones.

execution.attacker_perspective: A bound LDAP principal on a large directory.
payloads: Repeated compare ops on any DN (e.g. memberOf or uid compares against the app base)
instructions: Bind an LDAP app credential.
Send compare operations in a loop; each materialises the entire app view.
With bind-groups configured, each op additionally pays the O(users x groups x members) view filter.
execution.observed_result: Per-op isolate CPU proportional to full directory size; sustained ops degrade the isolate serving other requests.

remediation.strategy: Build only the compare target entry (index candidates by normalised DN), add executeCompare's deadline check, cache the derived DirectoryView alongside the snapshot, and pre-index group members as Sets.

code_changes.fixed_code: In candidateEntries, resolve the target DN first and build only that entry; reuse the executeSearch deadline.
members.get(g.id) -> Set; build visibleUserIds via `new Set(visibleMemberIds)` intersection instead of per-user scans.

likelihood.reason: One credential and repeated ops - no race or capture needed; reach limited to deployments exposing LDAP.

impact.reason: Isolate CPU burn bounded by the worker's CPU limit and per-connection op cap; degrades co-tenant requests on the isolate rather than breaking a boundary.

confidence.reason: The full materialisation and the missing deadline are directly readable in search.ts; the quadratic filter is visible in directory.ts.

title: Managed domains accept arbitrary strings; a suffix domain such as "com" captures brand resolution for unrelated hostnames (brandDomainForHost suffix match), and wildcard domains break deleteDomain's in-use LIKE
description: Every write path into the domains table stores String(value).trim().toLowerCase() with no DNS-name format check: POST /admin/domains (routes/admin.ts:4805-4812), POST /admin/setup (admin.ts:965-971), POST /api/v1/domains (api.ts:189-195), and runSetup (services/setup.ts:124-129). The column itself is TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE with no CHECK (migrations/0001_schema.sql:79-84). The read side assumes DNS-shaped values: domainFromHint enforces ^[a-z0-9](?:[a-z0-9.-]*[a-z0-9])?$ (brands.ts:143-148), so hint-driven lookups can never express the malformed values a writer can store. brandDomainForHost (brands.ts:188-203) resolves the brand for a request hostname by an exact match OR a dot-suffix match ('.' || domain) ordered by longest domain first. A domains:write principal can therefore add domain "com" (or any public-suffix-like or parent string), attach a brand to it, and any hostname ending in ".com" that reaches the Worker but matches no longer branded domain renders that entry's brand (logo, app name, colours, custom CSS) on its sign-in pages instead of the default brand. Under the designed multi-hostname deployment (branded custom domains are the documented purpose of brandDomainForHost) this overrides the branding visitors see on hostnames belonging to other managed-but-unbranded domains. Secondary, deployment-independent effects: deleteDomain's in-use guard interpolates the stored domain into a LIKE pattern (domains.ts:47 and :54-56, '%@' || domain / '%@' + domain), so stored '%' or '_' characters act as wildcards and make the domain undeletable while unrelated users exist (self-inflicted availability); applyDomainToAllUsers writes `${localPart}@${domain}` verbatim (domains.ts:86), so a malformed domain mints malformed UPNs (super-gated); a malformed domain set as default makes bare-username logins resolve to unusable UPNs. The trust tier is domains:write (delegatable to non-super admin roles and API keys), not super.
claimed_root_cause: addDomain (src/lib/domains.ts) and all five callers trim+lowercase the domain but never check it against a DNS-name grammar, while consumers (brandDomainForHost suffix matching, deleteDomain LIKE patterns, UPN construction, domainFromHint charset) all assume the invariant that a domains row is a well-formed DNS name.

trace.scope: admin.post /admin/domains (also api.ts:189-195 POST /api/v1/domains, admin.ts:965-971 /admin/setup, services/setup.ts:124-129 runSetup)
trace.description: domain = String(body.domain).trim().toLowerCase(); only non-empty is required before addDomain.
A malformed domain can also be promoted to default (existence check only), steering bare-username UPN resolution.
Stored domain interpolated into LIKE pattern '%@'||domain: '%' and '_' act as wildcards.
UPN minted as `${localPart}@${domain}` verbatim (super-gated).
SELECT domain ... domain = ?1 OR substr(?1,-(length(domain)+1)) = '.'||domain ORDER BY length(domain) DESC — a stored suffix like 'com' resolves for every .com host with no longer branded match.

evidence.description: CREATE TABLE domains: domain TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE — no CHECK constraint (migrations/0001_schema.sql:79-84).
await addDomain(c.env, domain) after only trim().toLowerCase() and a truthiness test.
domainFromHint is the only DNS-name grammar in the codebase and is read-side only; nothing applies it (or an equivalent) on writes.
brandDomainForHost dot-suffix match: stored domain 'com' resolves host 'anything.com'.

blockers: The brand-capture effect only matters when the Worker serves sign-in pages on hostnames other than the issuer (per-brand custom domains / Cloudflare for SaaS custom hostnames). Under a single-hostname deployment the residual is self-inflicted config breakage (wildcard LIKE refusals, unusable default/UPNs), which is below finding threshold on its own.
No local environment configured to confirm which hostname classes route to this Worker.

validation_plan.local: Seed the local D1 (wrangler d1 execute --local) with a domains row ('com', brand_id set to a custom brand) and request /login against `wrangler dev` with Host: unrelated.com; observe the custom brand rendered. The SQL semantics are already source-evident.
validation_plan.deployment: Check wrangler.jsonc routes/custom-domain configuration (and any Cloudflare for SaaS custom hostnames) to determine whether non-issuer hostnames reach the Worker; if they do, the brand-capture half is confirmed.

title: Audit chain verification cannot detect tail truncation or full-chain deletion: newest-row deletions leave a self-consistent chain, and an emptied log reports ok/empty
description: verifyAuditChain recomputes chain_hash over a bounded window of the newest rows and reports ok/broken/fork. Two blind spots are inherent to the design as implemented: (1) deleting the newest K chained rows leaves the remaining chain perfectly valid - verification reports 'ok' with a smaller 'checked' count, and there is no persisted head checkpoint to compare against; (2) deleting every chained row returns status 'ok' whenever unchained (pre-chain) rows remain, and 'empty' otherwise - indistinguishable from a fresh install. A related edge: fork-detection compares a mismatched row's hash only against seenHashes seeded with [""] plus verified rows - the window seed row's hash is never added, so a genuine fork whose parent is the seed row is reported 'broken' instead of 'fork'. Tamper-evidence against interior edits/deletions works; edge truncation does not.
root_cause: src/lib/audit.ts:82-134 verifies only what remains in the table (ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?); the genesis/head hash is never anchored or compared to an external expectation, so the absence of rows is invisible to the verifier.
intended_behavior: The verify endpoint is meant to answer 'was the log tampered with'; tail truncation is the most natural tamper for an attacker cleaning recent activity, and the API contract (ok/broken/fork) does not signal it.

trace.description: audit:read holder invokes verification over the newest <=10k rows.
Only surviving rows are read; deleted rows leave no residue to check.
All chained rows deleted + unchained rows remain => status 'ok' ('No chained rows to verify.'); all rows deleted => 'empty'.

evidence.description: Verification window is a LIMIT over current table contents.
status 'ok' returned when chained rows are absent but any rows exist.
seenHashes seeds with [""] only - the shifted-out seed row's stored hash is absent, so a fork parented on the seed is misreported 'broken'.

conditions.description: Tamper requires write access to D1 outside the app (the threat model the chain addresses); an interior edit IS detected - this is about deletions at the chain edges.

execution.attacker_perspective: An attacker (or negligent operator) with direct database write, e.g. wrangler d1 execute.
payloads: DELETE FROM audit_log WHERE id > (SELECT MAX(id)-50 FROM audit_log)
DELETE FROM audit_log WHERE chain_hash IS NOT NULL
instructions: Delete the newest chained rows, or every chained row while a pre-chain (NULL chain_hash) row remains.
GET /api/v1/audit/verify -> 'ok' (or 'empty'), with no signal that rows vanished.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified algorithm; no anchor exists that could flag absent rows.

remediation.strategy: Anchor the chain head: persist a daily/periodic checkpoint (e.g. an 'audit.checkpoint' row whose details carry the current head hash and max id) or emit the head hash to an external sink (SSF/event), so verification can distinguish 'no new rows' from 'rows deleted'. At minimum, document the truncation blind spot in the verify response ('checked' + max id returned) and include the seed row's hash in seenHashes so boundary forks report 'fork' correctly.

likelihood.reason: Requires raw database write - a higher tier than any API principal; an attacker at that tier could also recompute the whole chain (the design is evidence, not proof).

impact.reason: Newest-activity deletions and full-chain wipes go unreported by the verifier designed to catch tampering; interior tamper remains detected.

confidence.reason: The verification algorithm is fully readable; the blind spots follow directly from windowing + no head anchor.

title: HTTPS-only guard applies only while the issuer is unresolved - after setup (or with ISSUER_URL pinned) the entire IdP is served over plain HTTP
description: withResolvedIssuer is documented as enforcing 'FlareID only answers over HTTPS' (plus http on localhost for wrangler dev), but that refusal lives inside the issuer-derivation fallback and is skipped whenever an issuer already exists. src/lib/issuer.ts:67 returns the env untouched when the ISSUER_URL var is pinned; at line 68 `storedIssuer(env)` short-circuits `acceptableOrigin(request.url)` whenever the issuer_url row exists - which is every deployment after first-run setup (markSetupCompleted writes it, src/lib/settings.ts:178). Result: a request that arrives at the Worker over plain http:// is passed to the full app - the login page and password POST (/login, src/routes/login.ts), client_secret_basic and bearer tokens (/token, /api/v1/*, /scim/v2), SAML/OIDC flows, authorization codes in redirects. The Secure flag on the session cookie (src/lib/sessions.ts:71) prevents cookie storage/sending over http, but it does not protect the credentials themselves: a network MITM sees the password in the POST body, the API key / client secret in the Authorization header, and can replace the served login page. The Strict-Transport-Security header is set on the (already-cleartext) response at src/lib/security-headers.ts:89 and is ignored by browsers on http responses - and there is no redirect or refusal. The 400 'FlareID only answers over HTTPS' response (issuer.ts:70-73) is only reachable in the narrow pre-setup window with no pinned var.
root_cause: src/lib/issuer.ts:66-76 places the scheme check inside acceptableOrigin(), which is only evaluated in the `??` fallback after `env.ISSUER_URL` (line 67) and `storedIssuer(env)` (line 68) both miss. Once either issuer source exists the request is dispatched to app.fetch regardless of scheme - the intended https-only invariant is enforced only in the one state (pre-setup, no pin) where it matters least.
intended_behavior: Per the file's own contract - 'it is still only accepted over https - plus plain http for localhost, for wrangler dev' - a non-localhost http:// request should receive the 400 (or a 308 to https) on every request, not just when issuer derivation needs the request origin.

trace.description: Every HTTP request goes through withResolvedIssuer(env, request); a returned env is dispatched to the whole app.
`if (env.ISSUER_URL) return env;` - pinned var serves any scheme.
`(await storedIssuer(env)) ?? acceptableOrigin(request.url)` - a stored issuer short-circuits; acceptableOrigin (the only scheme check) is never evaluated post-setup.
login form + password POST, /token client auth, /api/v1 bearer keys, /authorize flows all served over http.

evidence.description: Pinned ISSUER_URL returns env without any scheme check.
Stored issuer (always present post-setup) satisfies `??`, so acceptableOrigin - the only place scheme is tested - is skipped.
The only https/http decision: https allowed, http only on localhost. Unreachable when an issuer is already known.
The 400 'FlareID only answers over HTTPS' refusal exists but only fires when no issuer resolves at all.
HSTS is emitted on every response but is ineffective on the cleartext response itself and on non-browser clients.
Session cookie is Secure+HttpOnly+SameSite=Lax - protects the cookie, not the password POST or Authorization headers.
No routes/custom domains declared: default deployment is a workers.dev Worker, which receives plain-HTTP requests (no platform redirect to https).

conditions.description: The Worker is reachable over http:// - the default for <name>.workers.dev (the edge does not auto-redirect http to https) and for custom domains whose zone does not enable 'Always Use HTTPS' (default off).
An attacker able to observe or modify network traffic on the victim's path (hostile Wi-Fi, on-path actor).

execution.attacker_perspective: On-path network attacker between a user or API client and the Cloudflare edge, on a deployment reachable over http (workers.dev default, or a custom domain without Always Use HTTPS).
payloads: GET http://<deployment-host>/login - the full login page is served; a password POST to http://<deployment-host>/login carries the credentials in cleartext.
POST http://<deployment-host>/token with client_secret_basic / Authorization: Bearer flareid_sk_... - machine credentials transit in cleartext.
instructions: On a deployment with a stored issuer (or pinned ISSUER_URL), request http://<host>/login - observe a 200 login page, not the 400 'FlareID only answers over HTTPS'.
Interpose on a victim's http request to observe the password POST or Authorization header; alternatively ssl-strip a first-time visitor and replace the page.
Contrast: http://<host>/ pre-setup (no stored issuer) is refused with the 400 - demonstrating the guard exists but is unreachable once an issuer is known.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified: once storedIssuer() returns a row (always true post-setup) or ISSUER_URL is set, no code path inspects request.url's scheme before dispatching to the full application. The intended https-only refusal is unreachable.

remediation.strategy: Enforce the scheme invariant for every request, independent of issuer resolution. In withResolvedIssuer, check acceptableOrigin(request.url) for http:// requests BEFORE the pinned/stored short-circuits: reject any non-localhost http request with the existing 400 (or 308 redirect to the same URL on https), regardless of which issuer source is used.

likelihood.reason: HTTP delivery to the Worker is the platform default on workers.dev and default-off 'Always Use HTTPS' on custom domains; exploitation additionally needs an on-path attacker and a victim on a cleartext first request.

impact.reason: Cleartext exposure of passwords, client secrets and API keys plus page substitution under MITM; Secure cookies prevent session-cookie capture but not request-credential theft. Real consequence but confined to http-using victims.

confidence.reason: The code path is fully source-verified: no scheme check is reachable once an issuer exists. Workers delivering http:// requests on workers.dev is documented platform behavior; a custom-domain deployment depends on a zone toggle.

title: login.failed audit rows carry the raw submitted identifier but the auto-flag counts by canonical UPN - spelling variants (case, spaces, username vs UPN) fully evade the failed-sign-in watchlist trigger
description: POST /login resolves the identifier to the account (getUserByLoginIdentifier normalizes trim/lowercase and also accepts bare usernames and aliases), but logAudit writes 'login.failed' with the raw submitted `upn` string as target. The auto-flag then counts audit_log rows where target = user.upn (canonical). Every spelling variant that still resolves to the same account - 'ADA@x.com', ' ada@x.com ', 'ada' vs 'ada@x.com', or an alias email - produces login.failed rows under a different target, so the >=10-per-hour threshold against the canonical UPN is never reached and the risk-watchlist flag never fires. The per-account rate bucket (loginRateKey) is canonicalized and still applies, so this is a detection-evasion bug, not a rate-limit bypass: a low-and-slow password guessing campaign stays invisible to the account-level watchlist control that exists specifically to catch it.
root_cause: src/routes/login.ts:311 logs `login.failed` with the un-normalized submitted identifier while src/routes/login.ts:316 counts rows filtered on the canonical user.upn - the two sides of the detection loop key on different strings.
intended_behavior: Attempts that resolve to the same account must all count toward that account's failure threshold: log the canonical user.upn (or the resolved loginRateKey) as the audit target when the identifier resolved to a user.

trace.description: upn taken verbatim from the form, only length-capped.
Lookup normalizes trim/lowercase and accepts bare username, UPN, or any listed email - many spellings resolve to one account.
logAudit 'login.failed' target = raw submitted string, not the resolved user's upn.
COUNT(*) WHERE action='login.failed' AND target = user.upn - variant-spelled rows never match, so fails >= 10 is unreachable under spelling rotation.

evidence.description: logAudit(c.env, null, 'login.failed', upn, ...) uses the raw `upn` variable from the request body.
The flag count binds user.upn (canonical, lowercase) - a different string than was written.
identifier.trim().toLowerCase() proves variants still resolve to the same account (and bare usernames resolve at line 23).
loginRateKey shows the codebase knows the bucket must bind to the account, not the spelling - the audit target was not given the same treatment.

conditions.description: None - the password step is anonymous; only a resolvable account name is needed.
Detection effect requires nothing else to be configured; only the downstream block value depends on Cloudflare One/SCIM syncs being enabled.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous caller password-guessing a known account who wants to avoid tripping the risk-watchlist flag.
payloads: POST /login bodies alternating upn spellings: 'ada@corp.com', 'ADA@CORP.COM', ' ada@corp.com ', 'ada' (bare username), each resolving to the same user
instructions: Run failed password attempts against the account while rotating case/whitespace/identifier form each window (5 attempts per 15 minutes under the default policy).
Inspect audit_log: login.failed rows exist under several distinct target values, none equal to the canonical user.upn in the required count of 10/hour.
user_watch / the Risk watchlist group never gain the account despite the sustained guessing burst.
execution.observed_result: audit_log fills with login.failed under non-canonical targets; COUNT for target=user.upn stays below 10; flagUser never fires - the account-level detection is bypassed while the per-account rate bucket still throttles attempts.

remediation.strategy: Write the canonical account identity to the audit target when resolution succeeded: at login.ts:311 use `user ? user.upn : upn.trim().toLowerCase()` (or the loginRateKey), matching the key the counter at :316 binds. Apply the same canonicalization to login.rate_limited at :290.

code_changes.fixed_code: await logAudit(c.env, null, "login.failed", user?.upn ?? upn.trim().toLowerCase(), { ip }, c.req.raw);

likelihood.reason: Trivial and free: any spelling mutation defeats the counter while still reaching the account; no privilege or timing sensitivity.

impact.reason: Only the account-level watchlist detection is evaded; rate limits still bound guessing and the IP-based auth-fail list still sees the source. The flag's downstream effect additionally needs CF One/SCIM wiring.

confidence.reason: Both sides of the comparison read directly; normalization in the lookup path confirms variants resolve to the same user.

title: Cloudflare Analytics Engine fetches in metrics.ts have no timeout - a hung upstream API call leaves admin performance/reporting requests waiting indefinitely
description: All four Analytics Engine SQL calls in src/lib/metrics.ts (lines 71, 97, 172, 215) issue `fetch('https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/.../analytics_engine/sql', ...)` with no AbortSignal/timeout. They run on the admin performance dashboard and GET /api/v1/performance (performance:read scope - a delegable permission) via services/monitoring.ts:191-196. If api.cloudflare.com stalls or a socket hangs, the request waits until outer platform timeouts, and each waiting request holds isolate resources; a caller with performance:read can queue repeated calls to pin the worker. A sibling gap on the federation plane is already recorded (flareid:federation.ts:oidc-outbound-fetches-no-timeout, needs_validation) - this is the same defect on the admin-tier metrics path.
claimed_root_cause: src/lib/metrics.ts:71,97,172,215 call fetch() without AbortSignal.timeout or a raced deadline.

trace.description: Calls readPerformanceSeries + readPerformance concurrently.
No timeout on the outbound API call.

evidence.description: First of four identical unguarded fetch sites (lines 71, 97, 172, 215).
overviewStats fans out 16+ D1 queries per dashboard load; the AE calls are the unbounded part.

blockers: Deployment-dependent: only fires when Analytics Engine is configured (CF_ACCOUNT_ID etc.), and the practical hang duration depends on platform subrequest behaviour, which cannot be established from source alone.
Real-world severity (whether a stalled fetch pins the isolate long enough to matter vs being cut by an outer timeout) needs a live or simulated-slow-upstream test.

validation_plan.local: Confirm no AbortSignal/timeout wrapper exists anywhere in metrics.ts and that monitoring.ts performance paths invoke it without a raced deadline (done - verified by read).
validation_plan.deployment: On a deployment with AE configured, make api.cloudflare.com unreachable (or inject a stalled response) and issue GET /api/v1/performance with a performance:read key; measure request lifetime and concurrent-hang behaviour.

title: Anonymous caller can make the Worker issue arbitrary outbound HTTPS GETs via self-registered jwks_uri (blind SSRF, unauthenticated trigger)
description: POST /connect/register is open to the internet and lets the registrant store an arbitrary https jwks_uri on a confidential client (registration.ts:153 stores it after the https-scheme-only validFrontchannelUri check). From then on, every unauthenticated POST to /token, /introspect, /revoke or /device_authorization that presents that client_id together with any parseable client_assertion causes verifyClientAssertion (src/lib/oauth-client-auth.ts:25-31) to run createRemoteJWKSet against the stored URL - an outbound GET from the Worker before any credential check succeeds. Mitigations verified in the vendored jose 6.2.12 remote.js: redirect:'manual' (no redirect following, so the write-time https check cannot be laundered through a redirect), a 5 s AbortSignal.timeout, a 200-status requirement, and the response is only JSON-parsed as a JWKS and never echoed to the caller. When the remote document is fetched successfully it is cached for 10 minutes per isolate (cacheMaxAge 600000); when the fetch fails the entry stays unset so every subsequent attempt triggers a fresh outbound request. The result is a blind, unauthenticated outbound-GET primitive: usable for reflected traffic at 1:1, for hitting GET endpoints with side effects, and for probing reachability/timing of public https origins from Cloudflare edge egress. Private-address reachability is bounded by the Workers platform (fetch to RFC1918/link-local generally cannot route), which is a deployment fact. [Merged duplicate record(s): h-oidc-07.]
root_cause: verifyClientAssertion (src/lib/oauth-client-auth.ts:28) hands the verbatim stored, caller-registered jwks_uri to createRemoteJWKSet on every client-assertion verification, and the fetch is reachable entirely before authentication - the only write-time gate is the https scheme check at registration.ts:153 / services/clients.ts:7-13.
intended_behavior: Outbound fetches should be initiated only for authenticated or operator-configured purposes. If private_key_jwt over remote JWKS is supported, the fetch should be rate-bounded per caller, restricted after registration-time review, or performed only after the client has otherwise authenticated.

trace.description: An unauthenticated registrant stores jwks_uri=https://attacker-chosen on a new confidential client (scheme checked to https only).
A later unauthenticated request presenting the client_id and any client_assertion (header-parseable JWT, signature need not be valid) routes into verifyClientAssertion.
createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(client.jwks_uri)) issues an outbound GET to the stored URL; on fetch failure it retries on every request, on success it caches 10 min per isolate.

evidence.description: client.jwks_uri branch constructs and caches a createRemoteJWKSet per URI in module-scope remoteJwks Map; the keyset is reloaded whenever no valid local set exists, so each failed-fetch attempt is a new outbound request.
Anonymous registration persists jwks_uri after only the https-scheme check (validFrontchannelUri, services/clients.ts:7-13); the same applies on RFC 7592 PUT update at registration.ts:202.

jose's fetchJwks uses redirect:'manual', a default 5 s timeout and requires status 200 plus JSON parse; the document is used only for key material and is never returned to the caller, bounding the primitive to a blind GET.

conditions.description: Impact depends on which origins are reachable from Cloudflare edge egress; private/link-local targets are expected to be unroutable from Workers but this is a deployment fact not in the repo.
Requires the open dynamic-registration endpoint to be reachable (it is mounted unconditionally in this source).

execution.attacker_perspective: Fully anonymous internet caller.
payloads: POST /connect/register {"redirect_uris":["https://rp.example/cb"],"token_endpoint_auth_method":"private_key_jwt","jwks_uri":"https://<chosen-target>/jwks.json"}
POST /token client_id=<new>&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer&client_assertion=<any header-parseable JWT>
instructions: Register a client whose jwks_uri points at an attacker-observed HTTPS endpoint (e.g. a request-bin or an origin under test).
Send any structurally valid client_assertion JWT (signature need not verify) to /token with that client_id.
Observe an inbound GET at the target from Cloudflare egress; repeat to generate one outbound GET per request whenever the target does not return a 200+JSON JWKS document.
execution.observed_result: Source-traced end to end: jwks_uri is stored verbatim by anonymous registration and fetched on each client-assertion verification attempt; jose's own code confirms no redirect follow, 5 s timeout, and that nothing of the response reaches the attacker.

remediation.strategy: Either perform the remote-JWKS fetch lazily only after an otherwise-authenticated client interaction, or constrain it: refuse jwks_uri on open dynamic registration (allow it only for operator-created clients), or front the fetch with per-caller/per-host rate limiting and a host allowlist posture consistent with the rest of the outbound-fetch inventory.

code_changes.fixed_code:
// Gate remote JWKS on clients the operator or a policy marked as vetted, or
// rate-limit remoteJwks misses per client_id before createRemoteJWKSet is invoked.

likelihood.reason: Trivially reachable anonymously: one registration plus one token request triggers the fetch; repeated triggers are unbounded except by the edge rate limiter.

impact.reason: Blind GET only: no response content is disclosed, no credentials are attached, redirects are not followed, and only public https origins are practically reachable; impact is reflector/probing value, not data access.

confidence.reason: Every hop verified in source including the vendored jose fetch implementation; the only unverifiable fact is egress reachability of private ranges, noted as a condition.

title: private_key_jwt client assertions never expire (no `exp` requirement) and are replayable indefinitely (no `jti` single-use store)
description: verifyClientAssertion (src/lib/oauth-client-auth.ts:36-41) verifies client_assertion JWTs with jose jwtVerify options that set only issuer, subject and audience. jose does not require the `exp` claim unless it is named in requiredClaims (verified against node_modules/jose/dist/webapi/lib/jwt_claims_set.js, presenceCheck built only from requiredClaims + aud + sub + iss), so a client assertion with no expiry verifies successfully and is valid forever; an assertion with a far-future exp is likewise accepted. FlareID stores no jti anywhere (no replay cache exists in the codebase), so the same assertion can be replayed an unlimited number of times. The result holds at every endpoint authenticateClient() guards: POST /token (token.ts:38), POST /introspect (introspect.ts:13), POST /revoke (introspect.ts:97) and POST /device_authorization (device.ts:62). Because `aud` accepts the bare ISSUER_URL, one assertion is replayable across all of them. Empirically verified locally with the vendored jose 6.2.12: a SignJWT assertion lacking exp passed jwtVerify under the identical option set, and a 10-year-exp assertion passed on repeated attempts. RFC 7523 section 3 lists `exp` as a REQUIRED claim for the client assertion and recommends bounded lifetimes plus optional jti replay protection. [Merged duplicate record(s): h-oidc-04.]
root_cause: jwtVerify is called at src/lib/oauth-client-auth.ts:41 without `requiredClaims: ["exp", "jti"]`, `maxTokenAge`, or any jti replay store; jose's claims validator only checks exp/iat/nbf when present, so absent-exp assertions pass and previously-seen assertions re-verify every time.
intended_behavior: Per RFC 7523 (JWT Profile for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication) the authorization server should require `exp` on client assertions, reject unreasonably long lifetimes, and may record `jti` to make assertions single-use. The intended control is that a client assertion is a short-lived, one-shot proof of possession, not a permanent bearer credential.

trace.description: Unauthenticated caller supplies client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer and client_assertion in the form body.
When no client_secret is presented, the assertion is forwarded to verifyClientAssertion for a confidential client.
jwtVerify(assertion, keySet, {issuer, subject, audience}) with no exp/jti/maxTokenAge constraints; a return of true authenticates the caller as the client at all four endpoints.

evidence.description: JWTVerifyOptions sets only issuer=client_id, subject=client_id, audience=[ISSUER_URL, ISSUER_URL+'/token']; no requiredClaims, no maxTokenAge, no algorithms allowlist, no jti handling.
presenceCheck is built only from requiredClaims, aud, sub, iss (and iat when maxTokenAge is set); exp is never required and is validated only when present, so an exp-less assertion verifies.
No jti store, KV lookup, or seen-assertion set exists in the file or anywhere in src/ (grep for jti finds only LDAP/SAML code); identical assertions re-verify on every request.

conditions.description: The attacker must obtain one valid client_assertion for a confidential client that registered jwks or jwks_uri - e.g. captured from a proxy/log that recorded the POST body, or a client that mints long-lived or exp-less assertions.
At least one confidential client must have jwks or jwks_uri registered (anyone can create such a client through the open POST /connect/register endpoint).

execution.attacker_perspective: A network/log observer holding one previously-issued client_assertion for a confidential client, or testing whether exp-less assertions are accepted.
payloads: POST /token grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=<victim>&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer&client_assertion=<captured JWT>
client_assertion minted without an `exp` claim (iss=sub=client_id, aud=<issuer>)
instructions: Register any client via POST /connect/register with token_endpoint_auth_method=private_key_jwt and a jwks document, obtaining its client_id.
Mint an RS256 client assertion containing iss, sub, aud, iat but no exp; POST it to /token and observe it authenticate (a grant-specific error such as invalid_grant proves authentication succeeded).
Replay the identical assertion repeatedly and against /introspect and /revoke; every attempt is accepted because no jti store exists.
Alternatively capture one legitimate client_assertion and replay it at any later time; it remains valid as long as its exp (if any) has not passed - indefinitely if the minting client omitted exp.
execution.observed_result: Local verification with the vendored jose 6.2.12 under the exact option object from oauth-client-auth.ts:36-41: an assertion with no `exp` claim verified successfully, and a single 10-year-exp assertion verified on repeated attempts. Source review confirms FlareID adds no jti store or replay check of its own.

remediation.strategy: Enforce short-lived, single-use client assertions in verifyClientAssertion: require `exp` and `jti` (requiredClaims), cap assertion age via maxTokenAge (e.g. "5m"), and record verified jti values in SESSIONS_KV (key `pkjwt-jti:<client_id>:<jti>`, TTL = assertion lifetime) refusing repeats.

likelihood.reason: Exploitation requires obtaining a valid client_assertion (TLS protects transit; capture happens via logs/traces) or a client that mints exp-less assertions; either precondition is plausible but not given.

impact.reason: A replayed assertion authenticates as the client at /token, /introspect, /revoke and /device_authorization - full client impersonation bounded to that one client's grant capabilities, potentially permanent when exp was omitted.

confidence.reason: Verified two ways: source review of both the FlareID call site and the vendored jose claims validator, plus a local execution check under the identical options showing no-exp acceptance and unlimited replay acceptance.

title: /check_session renders a per-session inline script through scriptTag(), permanently growing the CSP script-src hash list (and module memory) for every HTML response
description: The OP check-session iframe page builds its inline script with the session-specific OP_SID interpolated (src/routes/oidc-session.ts:102-112) and emits it via scriptTag(script) (line 114). scriptTag() adds each distinct script text to a module-global Set, and applySecurityHeaders() emits a CSP script-src containing a sha256 hash for EVERY script ever recorded in the isolate (src/lib/html.ts:881-897, src/lib/security-headers.ts:135-149). Each distinct user session that loads the iframe therefore permanently adds ~52 bytes to the CSP script-src of every subsequent HTML response in that isolate, and ~700 bytes of script text to the retained Set. The list is never pruned; there is no cap.
root_cause: scriptTag() was designed for a small fixed set of static scripts ('The scripts are fixed strings in this codebase - never built from request data', html.ts:874-879). /check_session violates that invariant by passing per-session data through it, making the global allowlist grow without bound.
intended_behavior: CSP hash allowlists must be finite. A per-request script needs a different mechanism (e.g., reading OP_SID from a data attribute or a JSON endpoint) rather than a distinct hashed inline script per session.

trace.description: Builds `var OP_SID=${JSON.stringify(sid)}` per request and calls scriptTag(script) at line 114.
INLINE_SCRIPTS.add(js) - module-scope Set retained for the isolate lifetime; one entry per unique session sid.
script-src ${[...(await inlineScriptHashes()), ...]} on every text/html response - includes every hash ever recorded, so the header grows monotonically.

evidence.description: const script = `var OP_SID=${JSON.stringify(sid)}; ...` - unique per session.
const INLINE_SCRIPTS = new Set(); SCRIPT_HASHES = new Map() - module scope, no eviction.
return [...SCRIPT_HASHES.values()] - every recorded hash is emitted, not just this response's scripts.

conditions.description: Multiple distinct user sessions loading the check-session iframe over one isolate's lifetime (any deployment with real OIDC session-management RPs).
Worker isolate lifetime and proxy/browser response-header size limits determine when growth becomes a failure.

execution.attacker_perspective: Any signed-in user whose RP embeds the iframe adds a permanent entry; growth is otherwise organic, not attacker-controlled (sessions require login).
payloads: GET /check_session with a valid session cookie.
instructions: Run the worker locally, create two sessions, load /check_session under each.
Inspect the Content-Security-Policy header of any subsequent HTML response: it contains one 'sha256-...' source per session script rendered, growing monotonically.
execution.observed_result: Source-verified unbounded growth of INLINE_SCRIPTS/SCRIPT_HASHES and of the emitted script-src list; the concrete failure threshold (header-size limit) is deployment-dependent.

remediation.strategy: Stop putting per-session data inside scriptTag(): serve OP_SID via a data attribute on a fixed script, a same-origin JSON fetch, or a postMessage handshake, so the inline script text is constant. Alternatively cap/evict the hash list, but a fixed script is the honest fix.

code_changes.fixed_code:
const script = `var OP_SID=document.getElementById("op").textContent; ...` and render
${escapeHtml(sid)}
- the script is then static.

likelihood.reason: Requires only normal RP iframe polling across distinct sessions; growth is guaranteed but its rate depends on session churn and isolate lifetime.

impact.reason: Availability-oriented degradation (bloated CSP header on every HTML page, isolate memory growth). No confidentiality or integrity impact; hashes are opaque.

confidence.reason: The growth mechanism is fully visible in source; only the breaking threshold is environmental.

title: Inbound photo fetch follows redirects off the verified https URL and buffers the entire body before the 1 MB cap - a provisioner URL can drive unbounded isolate memory use (and off-origin/cleartext fetches)
description: applyInboundPhoto (src/lib/photos.ts:71-94) implements the SCIM photos attribute: a data URI, or an https URL fetched server-side. For URLs it requires the submitted value to start with 'https://' (line 80) but then calls fetch(value, { cf: { cacheTtl: 0 } }) (line 82) with default redirect behaviour ('follow'): a 30x can retarget the fetch to any other origin, any port, and plain http - the https check protects only the first hop (contrast src/lib/scim-client.ts:79-98, which follows redirects manually precisely to keep the request on the expected origin). There is also no AbortSignal timeout (scimFetch sets 10s) and, most concretely, the response body is read in full via res.arrayBuffer() (line 85) BEFORE the MAX_PHOTO_BYTES (1 MB) check at line 86: a provisioner-controlled endpoint can stream an unbounded body and each accepted SCIM write forces the Worker isolate to buffer it. Reachability: any inbound-provisioning credential (directory:write API key) supplies photos[].value on POST/PUT/PATCH /scim/v2/Users (scim-server.ts:314-317 -> applyColumns:347-349). The stored result is constrained to sniffed image types <=1MB served at /account/photo/:uid to signed-in users, so content exfiltration is bounded; the material impacts are (a) per-request unbounded memory/CPU consumption in the isolate (billing + head-of-line pressure on co-tenant requests, self-limiting per isolate in the Workers model), and (b) a server-side fetch primitive to arbitrary public URLs incl. redirect-downgraded cleartext - on non-Workers/self-hosted deployments this could reach internal endpoints, though no internal-IP audience is presumed here. Triggerable repeatedly (one fetch per write), and the URL can differ per request. [Merged duplicate record(s): h-ratelimit-06.]
root_cause: fetch() with default redirect handling plus a post-hoc size cap: the bound is enforced on the buffered ArrayBuffer instead of streaming with an early-abort, and no request timeout is set.
intended_behavior: A size-capped, same-origin (or at least https-locked), time-boxed fetch: redirect:'manual' with an origin/scheme check like scimFetch, AbortSignal.timeout, and a streamed read that aborts at MAX_PHOTO_BYTES+1 rather than buffering first.

trace.description: directory:write requester's photos[].value string becomes `photo` for applyColumns.
Non-empty photo value reaches applyInboundPhoto on every create/replace/patch/correlate path.
Default 'follow' redirects, no timeout signal - cross-origin and http-downgrade reachable.
Whole body buffered before the byteLength > MAX_PHOTO_BYTES check at line 86.

evidence.description: Only the submitted string is scheme-checked; redirect targets are unconstrained.
fetch with no redirect:'manual' and no AbortSignal - unlike scimFetch which implements both.
arrayBuffer() precedes the size test at line 86 - cap cannot bound memory.
The codebase's own comment/model for doing this correctly: manual same-origin redirect handling plus AbortSignal.timeout(10_000).

conditions.description: Any directory:write-capable SCIM credential (or mastered photo writes) - the documented provisioning tier.
Internal-network reachability from the fetch egress applies only to non-Workers deployments; on Cloudflare Workers the practical impact is isolate memory/time exhaustion plus public-URL fetch.

execution.attacker_perspective: HR/provisioning integration holding a directory:write key, able to write photos[].value on any user it may touch.
payloads: PATCH /scim/v2/Users/{id} {"Operations":[{"op":"replace","path":"photos","value":[{"value":"https://attacker.example/redirect-to-http-or-1gb-stream"}]}]}
instructions: Point photos[].value at an endpoint returning a >1MB (e.g. endless chunked) body: the Worker buffers it all before rejecting.
Or return a 302 to http://<other-host>/: the fetch follows off-origin and off-https despite the input check.
Repeat per SCIM write to amplify isolate memory pressure.
execution.observed_result: Full body buffered in isolate memory before the cap rejects storage; redirect leaves the https-verified URL. Source-verified; runtime effect is per-isolate bounded in the Workers model.

remediation.strategy: Mirror scimFetch's discipline: redirect:'manual' with same-origin (or https-only) hop validation, AbortSignal.timeout(~10s), and stream the body cancelling at MAX_PHOTO_BYTES+1 bytes.

likelihood.reason: Single authenticated provisioning request; no race or extra conditions. Impact ceiling is bounded on Workers.

impact.reason: Per-isolate memory/time exhaustion (self-limiting in the serverless model, though it bills and head-of-line-blocks), plus a low-value server-side fetch oracle; stored content must sniff as a real image so data exfiltration is minimal. Internal-network reach is deployment-dependent.

confidence.reason: Code paths are unambiguous; the comparison reference (scimFetch) demonstrates the intended hardening pattern in the same codebase.

title: Four credential classes sit plaintext in D1 while the sealed.ts at-rest pattern is applied only to LDAP bind secrets - including every user's TOTP seed
description: FlareID has a working AES-256-GCM at-rest seal (src/lib/sealed.ts) but applies it only to ldap_apps.secret_enc (src/ldap/apps.ts:67,82,90) and signing private JWKs. Every other recoverable credential class is stored as plaintext rows: (1) scim_targets.secret - the bearer token FlareID sends to downstream SCIM servers - is inserted raw at src/lib/scim-targets.ts:181 and rewritten raw at :238 (migrations/0034_scim_targets.sql:13 declares it TEXT NOT NULL and the migration copies the legacy idp_settings.scim_secret value into it unchanged at :35); (2) upstream_idps.config holds the OIDC client_secret inside plaintext JSON (migrations/0037_upstream_idps.sql:11; src/lib/federation.ts:97-103 builds it, :124/:139 write it); (3) users.totp_secret - the shared secret for every enrolled authenticator - is plaintext (migrations/0001_schema.sql:34; src/routes/account.ts:1263), so a D1 read clones every user's second factor; (4) idp_settings carries turnstile_secret (src/lib/settings.ts:287), cfone.api_token (src/lib/cfone.ts:74; the related export-surface issue is already recorded as cfone.api-token-plaintext-exported) and the optional shared default_password (src/lib/settings.ts:193). Read surfaces are correctly write-only (src/api/applications.ts:274-284,345-358 return secret_set booleans only), so the exposure is at-rest: direct D1/console access, the admin backup export, and the daily R2 snapshot that serialises the entire bundle (src/lib/backup.ts:157-163). backup.ts:13 describes that bundle as holding 'encrypted SCIM/API secrets' - true only of LDAP apps.
root_cause: Secret columns written before sealed.ts existed (and scim_targets/upstream_idps written after) were never migrated to the envelope: src/lib/sealed.ts is imported only by src/ldap/apps.ts, while scim-targets.ts:175-197 and federation.ts:97-140 bind raw secret strings into D1.
intended_behavior: Recoverable secrets the codebase itself treats as sensitive (it redacts them from every read API as secret_set booleans) should use the sealText/unsealText envelope like ldap_apps.secret_enc, or at minimum the snapshot/export path should not silently carry them plaintext to R2.

trace.description: Operator-supplied downstream SCIM credential is accepted and handed to createScimTarget.
input.secret.trim() is bound verbatim into INSERT INTO scim_targets - no sealing.
config JSON containing client_secret is bound verbatim into upstream_idps.
totp_secret written plaintext to the users row at enrolment confirm.
SELECT * per table serialises every plaintext secret into the JSON bundle; snapshotToR2 (line 161) writes it daily to the BACKUPS bucket when configured.

evidence.description: secret TEXT NOT NULL - a plaintext column, created after sealed.ts existed.
sealText used for ldap_apps secrets - the pattern exists and is deliberately scoped to LDAP only.
secret_set boolean returned instead of the value - the code treats these as secrets it must not disclose, yet stores them unprotected.
Comment claims the bundle contains 'encrypted SCIM/API secrets' - stale claim vs the plaintext columns.
totp_secret TEXT - per-user TOTP seeds plaintext at rest.

conditions.description: Exposure requires read access to D1, an exported backup bundle, or the R2 BACKUPS bucket - operator/platform-tier, not an API-scope escalation.
sealText returns null when no key material exists; Deploy-to-Cloudflare installs already ship KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY so sealing is available on real deployments.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anyone (insider, exfiltrated backup, compromised R2 bucket, or a future SQL-reading bug) holding the D1 rows or the daily snapshot.
payloads: Read scim_targets.secret / upstream_idps.config / users.totp_secret / idp_settings values from the dump.
instructions: Obtain the D1 database, a backup bundle from the admin backup export, or backups/YYYY-MM-DD.json from R2.
Read secrets directly: no decryption needed.
Use a downstream SCIM token against the target endpoint, an upstream client_secret at the IdP token endpoint, or a TOTP seed to generate valid second-factor codes for that user indefinitely.
execution.observed_result: All listed secrets recoverable verbatim from storage; TOTP seeds give durable second-factor bypass for every enrolled account.

remediation.strategy: Migrate each recoverable secret to the existing sealText envelope (new *_enc columns or sealed values in-place), decrypt lazily where consumers need the raw value, and correct the backup.ts comment. Distinct root from cfone.api-token-plaintext-exported (that record covers the cfone token's API-export surface; this covers the cross-table at-rest parity gap).

code_changes.fixed_code: Store `await sealText(env, secret)` in a secret_enc column and unseal where the client builds the Authorization header (scim-client.ts).
Seal client_secret within the config JSON (e.g. client_secret_enc) and unseal in oidcExchange.

likelihood.reason: Requires storage-tier access (D1, backup bundle, or R2 bucket) rather than an application path; that is precisely the tier the sealed construction was built for.

impact.reason: One dump yields downstream provisioning tokens, upstream IdP client credentials, and every enrolled TOTP seed - durable second-factor bypass at directory scale.

confidence.reason: Plaintext columns and the single-use scope of sealText are directly visible in migrations and source; redaction on read APIs is verified.

title: Legacy non-https SAML ACS/SLO endpoints are never re-validated: write-time https enforcement leaves pre-existing rows deliverable to cleartext or non-URL schemes
description: All current write paths now enforce https for ACS and SLO endpoints (api.ts:1071, api.ts:1094, admin.ts:4256, admin.ts:4288, sp-metadata.ts:61, sp-metadata.ts:91) and default_acs_url must be a member of acs_urls. But nothing re-checks scheme at use time or migrates stored rows: resolveAcsUrl (service-providers.ts:48-56) enforces membership only; the auto-POST form emits whatever URL is stored (post-form.ts:34); the SLO handler redirects the signed LogoutResponse to sp.slo_url verbatim (saml-slo.ts:44,109); and the refresh merge's keep-if-empty fallback (sp-metadata.ts:260) can re-store a sole non-https ACS indefinitely. Any saml_service_providers row written before the https enforcement existed (or written directly to D1) keeps working - a bearer assertion POSTed over http://, or a form action on a non-URL scheme.
claimed_root_cause: Scheme validation was added only at write boundaries; resolveAcsUrl and samlPostForm do not re-check scheme at use time, and no migration scrubs pre-existing rows.

trace.description: resolveAcsUrl returns the stored URL after an exact-match membership check only - no scheme verification at delivery time.
The stored ACS URL becomes the auto-submitting form's action verbatim (HTML-escaped only); a signed assertion is POSTed there without user confirmation.
302 to sp.slo_url verbatim - a stored non-https endpoint still receives the signed LogoutResponse.
When the publisher withdraws all endpoints, storedAcs is re-stored wholesale - including any non-https legacy entry, bypassing the https filter meta.acsUrls would otherwise impose.

evidence.description: Membership check only: `registered.includes(sp.default_acs_url)` and `registered[0]` - scheme never examined at read/use time.
https enforcement exists only in the write path for new values.
Same write-time-only enforcement in the console form parser.
Fallback re-stores stored acs_urls unfiltered when the merged list would be empty.

blockers: Whether the deployed D1 actually contains a saml_service_providers row with a non-https acs_urls entry, default_acs_url, or slo_url predating the validation is deployment state not visible in source.

Whether any such legacy value is also a non-URL scheme (e.g. javascript:) determines whether impact is cleartext delivery only or additionally auto-executing form-action script in browsers that still honor javascript: form actions.

validation_plan.local: Insert a saml_service_providers row directly into a dev D1 with acs_urls ["http://sp.example/acs"] and slo_url "http://sp.example/slo"; drive /saml/sso and observe the auto-POST form action and the SLO redirect target are emitted verbatim.
validation_plan.deployment: Run `SELECT id, acs_urls, default_acs_url, slo_url FROM saml_service_providers` on the deployed D1 (or `wrangler d1 execute`) and check for any entry not matching ^https://.

title: SCIM PUT/PATCH/POST-correlate: custom-attribute writes are merged into the row only after the admin-role-grant guard runs, so a directory:write key can rule-match a user into an admin-role group
description: The inbound SCIM server's anti-privilege-escalation guard assertNoAdminRoleGrant is supposed to evaluate the post-write user row against the rules of every dynamic group linked to an admin role (comment at src/routes/scim-server.ts:441-446: 'an attribute write can be an admin grant too'). On the three update paths - POST /scim/v2/Users correlation adopt (line 377), PUT /scim/v2/Users/:id (line 457) and PATCH /scim/v2/Users/:id (line 501) - the guard is called with {...user, ...cols, email} where `cols` contains only plain column writes. Custom schema-attribute writes are returned by columnsFrom as a separate `custom` map (line 319) and are folded into cols.custom_attributes inside applyColumns (lines 323-331) - i.e. strictly after the guard already ran against the stale custom_attributes JSON. Custom attributes are first-class rule fields: ruleFields() spreads both bare custom names and 'custom.<name>' into the matchable field set (src/lib/groups.ts:41-42), so a dynamic group whose rule matches on a custom attribute is a supported configuration. A SCIM API key holding only directory:write can therefore PATCH a mapped custom attribute (e.g. urn:...:Enterprise extension or any mapped attribute that applyUserMappings routes to custom.<key>) whose value satisfies the rule of a dynamic group linked to an admin role, granting the victim/attacker-controlled account that role's permissions undetected. The POST create path does it correctly - it merges custom into `after.custom_attributes` before grantsAdminRoleGroup (lines 409-416), and the directory-import and console services paths merge custom before the same check (src/lib/directory-import.ts:500-509,586-588; src/services/users.ts:269-287) - which proves the intended contract and makes the update-path omission a bug, not a design choice. holdsAdminRole still blocks writing to accounts that ALREADY hold an admin role, but it cannot see the grant the write itself creates.
root_cause: assertNoAdminRoleGrant(c, user, {...cols, ...}) is invoked before applyColumns merges the `custom` map into custom_attributes, so grantsAdminRoleGroup evaluates the pre-write custom_attributes; the fix is to merge custom into the `after` row before the check exactly as the POST-create path does (scim-server.ts:409-416).
intended_behavior: Every non-admin directory writer must be prevented from producing a post-write row that matches the rule of a dynamic group linked to an admin role - the same guarantee the POST create path, directory import and console user services already enforce.

trace.description: directory:write-scoped PATCH entry; patchToBody turns operations into a ScimUserBody, columnsFrom evaluates mappings over the merged document.
applyUserMappings returns mapped custom-attribute writes as a separate `custom` map; `cols` never contains custom_attributes at this point.
Guard receives {...cols, email-derived} - no custom_attributes merge; identical pattern at line 457 (PUT) and line 377 (POST correlation adopt).
grantsAdminRoleGroup(env, user, {...user, ...cols}) evaluates the user's OLD custom_attributes JSON against role-linked dynamic rules.
Only here is `custom` folded into cols.custom_attributes and written - after the guard has already passed.
Rule matching reads custom attribute values ({...custom, custom.<name>}), so a custom-attribute write can be the exact condition a role-linked rule tests.

evidence.description: assertNoAdminRoleGrant builds `after` as {...(user ?? {}), ...cols} - custom map not included.
applyColumns merges `custom` into cols.custom_attributes - the code that runs after the guard on every update path.
POST create path merges custom into after.custom_attributes BEFORE grantsAdminRoleGroup - the correct pattern the update paths omit.
userMatchesRule uses ruleFields which exposes custom attributes to rule conditions.
grantsAdminRoleGroup matches `after` against every dynamic group's rule linked to an admin role - the guard that is bypassed.
Import path merges mergedCustom into `after` before grantsAdminRoleGroup - sibling writers do this correctly.

conditions.description: A FlareID API key scoped directory:write (the documented HR/provisioning credential) - not admin-scoped.
A dynamic group linked to an admin role whose rule matches on a custom schema attribute (bare or custom.<name> form); supported, intended rule fields.
An inbound SCIM mapping (or standard attribute path) that routes the attacker-controlled SCIM value into the matching custom attribute - custom.<key> mapping targets exist for exactly this.

execution.attacker_perspective: Operator of an HR/provisioning integration holding a directory:write API key - a deliberately delegated, non-admin credential - who knows (or probes for) a role-linked dynamic group's rule field, e.g. custom.clearance = 'it-admin'.
payloads: PATCH /scim/v2/Users/{external_id} with Operations: [{"op":"replace","path":"urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:enterprise:2.0:User:clearance","value":"it-admin"}] where a mapping routes the attribute to custom.clearance
Equivalent PUT /scim/v2/Users/{id} body, or POST /scim/v2/Users whose userName correlates onto an existing non-admin user
instructions: As an admin, link a dynamic group with rule {"all":[{"field":"custom.clearance","op":"eq","value":"it-admin"}]} to any admin role, and add an inbound mapping target custom.clearance.
As the directory:write key, PATCH the mapped attribute value 'it-admin' onto a user the key controls.
Observe 200 and user_patched audit; accessFor(user.id) now reports the admin role - no 403 was raised.
execution.observed_result: The write is accepted (guard evaluated stale custom_attributes) and the user lands in the admin-role dynamic group; accessFor/grants now include the role's permissions. Source-verified; consistent with the POST-create path which does the merge first.

remediation.strategy: In assertNoAdminRoleGrant call sites (scim-server.ts:377, 457, 501) build the post-write row exactly as applyColumns will: merge `custom` onto the user's current custom_attributes JSON first, then evaluate grantsAdminRoleGroup. Cheapest correct fix: hoist the custom-merge block out of applyColumns into a shared helper used by both the guard input and the write.

likelihood.reason: Requires a directory:write API key - an intended delegation - plus a role-linked dynamic rule over a custom attribute and a mapping that feeds it. The rule/mapping combo is the supported use-case for custom attributes in dynamic groups; once present the exploit is one ordinary PATCH.

impact.reason: Escalates a non-admin provisioning credential to whatever the linked role grants (users/groups/domains write, up to '*' if Super Admin is dynamically linked) - precisely the boundary assertNoAdminRoleGrant exists to hold.

confidence.reason: Source-grounded: the merge order is explicit in code, the POST-create path demonstrates the intended order, and custom attributes are documented rule fields.

title: SCIM directory:write key can rename, re-populate, or delete the 'Risk watchlist' system group - the invariant every other writer enforces is missing on the SCIM-in plane
description: The inbound SCIM server's group mutation routes (PUT/PATCH/DELETE /scim/v2/Groups/:id, plus member adds/removes via PATCH) guard only admin-role groups: loadGroup(c, write) at scim-server.ts:520-524 checks `group.name === SUPER_ADMINS_GROUP || adminRoleGroupIds`, and memberStatements (591-603) checks `group.rule` (dynamic) and admin-member scope - but nothing checks `groups.system`. The Cloudflare One 'Risk watchlist' group is a system group (groups.system = 'watchlist', cfone.ts:284-289, created at 295) whose membership is meant to be maintained automatically from user_watch rows (flagUser cfone.ts:351-372 inserts the member row; reconcileWatchlist 333-348 re-derives the set hourly). A holder of any directory:write SCIM API key - a delegated provisioning credential that does not need the admin scope - can therefore: (a) PATCH/PUT replace members on the watchlist group, injecting arbitrary non-admin users into it or emptying it; the change is pushed to every outbound SCIM target immediately via downstream() -> pushGroupAndRemoved, and syncGroups pushes all groups with no system filter (scim-client.ts:803-806), so connected IdPs/apps consuming the 'Risk watchlist' group see attacker-chosen 'risky' users (or a stripped list) until the hourly reconcileWatchlist restores the true set - and the attacker can re-corrupt it each window; (b) PATCH/PUT displayName to rename the group (name changes are pushed downstream too); (c) DELETE the group outright - deleting the groups row, cascade-deleting all group_members, and queueing a remote deprovision for every linked SCIM target (scim-server.ts:683-687). Every other write path refuses this: services/groups.ts:150 blocks delete, :174/:190 block membership edits, :207 blocks managers on system groups; access.ts:56,135 excludes system groups from access requests. user_watch itself is untouched, so local watch state survives - the corruption is the externally-propagated group signal and the group's identity/deletion, and it silently self-heals locally which also hides the tampering.
root_cause: scim-server.ts implements group writes with raw SQL instead of the services/groups.ts layer, so the `groups.system` immutability invariant enforced at services/groups.ts:150,174,190,207 (and honored by access.ts:56,135 and cfone.ts's own lookup-by-system at :289) was never applied to the SCIM plane. loadGroup's write guard (scim-server.ts:523) enumerates only admin-role groups.
intended_behavior: System groups are internal machinery: their existence and membership are maintained by the owning feature (user_watch rows for 'watchlist').
